sections.heading: Sets, Venn Algebra & Counting of Relations
sections.summary: Set algebra translates logical inclusions into cardinalities via Inclusion-Exclusion, while relation counting on a finite set A of size n reduces to constrained binary matrices of size n x n. Distinguish reflexive, symmetric, antisymmetric, and equivalence counts cleanly before tackling bijection problems.
keyPoints: Power set & subsets: If |A| = n, |P(A)| = 2^n; proper subsets = 2^n - 1; non-empty proper subsets = 2^n - 2. Number of elements in A x B is |A|.|B|, and subsets of A x B (total relations from A to B) = 2^(|A||B|).

Set laws & Inclusion-Exclusion: De Morgan's Laws (A U B)' = A' intersect B' and (A intersect B)' = A' U B'; Symmetric difference A Delta B = (A - B) U (B - A). For 3 sets: n(A U B U C) = Sum n(A) - Sum n(A intersect B) + n(A intersect B intersect C).

Exact two-set / exact one-set counts: n(exactly 2 of A, B, C) = n(A intersect B) + n(B intersect C) + n(C intersect A) - 3 n(A intersect B intersect C); n(exactly 1) = Sum n(A) - 2 Sum n(A intersect B) + 3 n(A intersect B intersect C).

Relation counts on |A| = n: Total relations = 2^(n^2); Reflexive = 2^(n^2 - n); Irreflexive = 2^(n^2 - n); Symmetric = 2^(n(n+1)/2); Reflexive & Symmetric = 2^(n(n-1)/2); Antisymmetric = 2^n * 3^(n(n-1)/2).

Equivalence relations (Reflexive + Symmetric + Transitive): Count equals the Bell number B_n (number of partitions of an n-element set into non-empty equivalence classes): B_1 = 1, B_2 = 2, B_3 = 5, B_4 = 15, B_5 = 52.

Transitivity edge-case check: A relation with zero conflicting pairs (a, b) and (b, c) is VACUOUSLY transitive (e.g., {(1, 2)} is transitive, and the empty relation is symmetric & transitive, though NOT reflexive for n >= 1).

sections.heading: Functions: Domain, Range & Special Function Identities
sections.summary: Domain determination requires intersecting every algebraic, logarithmic, radical, and trigonometric restriction simultaneously, whereas Range demands monotonicity, quadratic discriminant, AM-GM, or graphical analysis. Greatest integer [x] and fractional part {x} introduce jump discontinuities that must be split unit-by-unit.
keyPoints: Core Domain constraints: (1) Even root sqrt(f(x)) requires f(x) >= 0; (2) Denominator g(x) != 0; (3) log_b(f(x)) requires f(x) > 0, b > 0, b != 1; (4) tan(u), sec(u) forbid u = (2k+1)pi/2; cot(u), cosec(u) forbid u = k*pi; (5) f(x)^g(x) in real analysis generally requires f(x) > 0.

Greatest Integer [x] & Fractional Part {x} = x - [x]: 0 <= {x} < 1; [x + n] = [x] + n and {x + n} = {x} for all integers n. Mirror identities: [x] + [-x] = 0 (if x in Z) else -1; {x} + {-x} = 0 (if x in Z) else 1.
Hermite's Identity: [x] + [x + 1/n] + [x + 2/n] + ... + [x + (n-1)/n] = [n x] for every positive integer n and real x. Essential for evaluating large step-function sums.

Range techniques: (1) For rational quadratic P(x)/Q(x) over R (with no common factor), set y = P(x)/Q(x), form quadratic in x, enforce Discriminant D >= 0, and check leading x^2 coefficient = 0 separately! (2) Express y = a cos x + b sin x in [-sqrt(a^2+b^2), sqrt(a^2+b^2)].
Signum sgn(x): sgn(x) = |x|/x for x != 0 and 0 for x = 0. Useful identity: |x| = x * sgn(x), and for polynomials f(x), sgn(f(x)) jumps only at roots of f(x).
Domain of f(x) + g(x) or f(x)/g(x): Domain(f +/- g) = D_f intersect D_g; Domain(f / g) = (D_f intersect D_g) \ {x : g(x) = 0}. Never cancel common factors before finding the domain!

sections.heading: Injective, Surjective, Bijective & Invertible Mappings
sections.summary: A function is invertible if and only if it is bijective (both one-one and onto on its stated codomain). On finite sets, counting onto mappings requires Inclusion-Exclusion, while on R -> R, calculus derivatives and odd/even polynomial degree properties decide bijectivity instantly.
keyPoints: One-One (Injective): Horizontal line y = c cuts graph at most once. For continuous functions on an interval, f is injective iff it is STRICTLY monotonic (f'(x) >= 0 or <= 0 with f'(x) = 0 only at isolated points, never on an entire sub-interval).

Even vs Odd polynomial check: Every even function defined on symmetric domain (-a, a) fails to be one-one (since f(-x) = f(x)). Every odd-degree real polynomial P(x) from R -> R is ALWAYS onto R (range = (-infinity, +infinity)), though not necessarily one-one.
Onto (Surjective): Range(f) MUST equal Codomain(f). If Codomain is restricted explicitly to Range(f), every function becomes onto; always read the stated codomain A -> B carefully.

Counting functions from |A| = m to |B| = n: Total functions = n^m. One-one functions = P(n, m) = n!/(n-m)! if m <= n, else 0. Onto functions (m >= n) = Sum_{k=0}^n (-1)^k C(n, k) (n - k)^m (for m < n, count = 0).

Pigeonhole bijection rule: For f: A -> A on a FINITE set |A| = n, f is one-one <=> f is onto <=> f is bijective (total bijections = n!). This equivalence FAILS on infinite sets (e.g., f(n) = 2n on N is one-one but not onto).

Inverse properties: (f^(-1)) graph is the reflection of f across y = x. Intersection points of f and f^(-1) ALWAYS include solutions of f(x) = x, PLUS possible symmetric pairs (a, b) & (b, a) when f is strictly DECREASING!

sections.heading: Composition, Periodicity, Parity & Graphical Transformations
sections.summary: Composite f(g(x)) requires g(x) to land inside Domain(f), making piecewise branch splitting mandatory when g(x) crosses boundary thresholds. Periodicity follows algebraic LCM rules on rational periods, while graphical shifts and modulus reflections reconstruct complex curves in seconds.
keyPoints: Composite domain & associativity: Domain(f o g) = {x in Domain(g) : g(x) in Domain(f)}. Composition is associative (f o (g o h) = (f o g) o h) but NOT commutative. If f, g are bijective, (f o g)^(-1) = g^(-1) o f^(-1).
Parity decomposition: Every function defined on a symmetric domain (-a, a) splits uniquely into Even + Odd: f(x) = [f(x) + f(-x)]/2 + [f(x) - f(-x)]/2. Only f(x) = 0 is both even and odd.

Standard fundamental periods: sin^n x, cos^n x, sec^n x, cosec^n x have period pi (n even) and 2*pi (n odd); tan^n x, cot^n x ALWAYS have period pi; |sin x| + |cos x| has period pi/2; {x} has period 1; constant functions are periodic with NO fundamental period.

Period algebra: If f(x) has period T, then f(ax + b) has period T / |a|. Period of f(x) + g(x) is LCM(T1, T2) if the LCM exists (rational ratio T1/T2 in Q); beware that symmetry cancellations can halve the LCM (e.g. |sin x| + |cos x| has period pi/2, not pi)!
Irrational period sum trap: Functions like sin(x) + cos(pi x) or {x} + sin(x) are NON-PERIODIC because the ratio of their periods (2*pi / 2 = pi, or 1 / (2*pi)) is irrational.
Graph transformations from y = f(x): y = f(|x|) keeps x >= 0 and mirrors it to x < 0; y = |f(x)| flips negative y-portions above x-axis; |y| = f(x) keeps f(x) >= 0 and mirrors across x-axis.

sections.heading: Functional Equations & Polynomial Signatures
sections.summary: Competitive functional equations rarely need brute-force guessing; instead, standard substitutions (x=0, y=0, y=-x, x->1/x, x->1-x) expose Cauchy signatures or symmetric pairing identities. Differentiating w.r.t. one variable while holding the other fixed turns continuous equations into elementary ODEs.
keyPoints: Cauchy's 4 classical signatures (assuming continuity or monotonicity on R): (1) f(x+y) = f(x) + f(y) => f(x) = k x; (2) f(x+y) = f(x) f(y) => f(x) = a^x (or 0); (3) f(xy) = f(x) + f(y) => f(x) = k ln|x|; (4) f(xy) = f(x) f(y) => f(x) = x^n (or 0).
Polynomial signature f(x) + f(1/x) = f(x) f(1/x) for x != 0: Equivalently (f(x) - 1)(f(1/x) - 1) = 1, forcing polynomial f(x) = 1 +/- x^n (or constant 2).
Reciprocal & linear fractional elimination: Given a f(x) + b f(1/x) = g(x), replace x -> 1/x to obtain a second linear equation and eliminate f(1/x) algebraically (valid when |a| != |b|).
Symmetry sum pairing f(x) + f(1 - x) = c: Classic template f(x) = a^x / (a^x + sqrt(a)) satisfies f(x) + f(1 - x) = 1, allowing instant pairing of k/N and (N - k)/N terms in sums.
Shift-periodicity functional equations: f(x + a) = -f(x) => period 2a; f(x + a) = 1 / f(x) => period 2a; f(x + a) = (1 + f(x))/(1 - f(x)) => period 4a; f(x+a) + f(x-a) = f(x) => period 6a.
Partial derivative trick: If f is differentiable and satisfies f(x+y) = f(x) + f(y) + h(x,y), differentiate w.r.t. y keeping x fixed, then set y = 0 to obtain f'(x) directly.

sections.heading: Inverse Trigonometric Functions (ITF): Principal Branches & Sums
sections.summary: Restricting trigonometric domains makes all six inverse functions single-valued, continuous, and monotonic on their principal ranges. Every addition formula carries strict product or sum thresholds where a +/- pi branch jump is mandatory.
keyPoints: Negative argument & complementary identities: sin^(-1)(-x) = -sin^(-1)x, tan^(-1)(-x) = -tan^(-1)x, cosec^(-1)(-x) = -cosec^(-1)x (odd); whereas cos^(-1)(-x) = pi - cos^(-1)x, cot^(-1)(-x) = pi - cot^(-1)x, sec^(-1)(-x) = pi - sec^(-1)x.
Complementary sums (ALWAYS hold on full domain): sin^(-1)x + cos^(-1)x = pi/2 (|x| <= 1); tan^(-1)x + cot^(-1)x = pi/2 (x in R); sec^(-1)x + cosec^(-1)x = pi/2 (|x| >= 1).
Outer-trig vs Inner-trig cancellations: sin(sin^(-1)x) = x ONLY for |x| <= 1; whereas sin^(-1)(sin x) is defined for ALL real x as a 2*pi-periodic piecewise linear sawtooth wave in [-pi/2, pi/2].
Piecewise tan^(-1)x + tan^(-1)y formula: Equal to tan^(-1)((x+y)/(1-xy)) if xy < 1; ADD +pi if x > 0, y > 0, xy > 1; SUBTRACT -pi if x < 0, y < 0, xy > 1; equals +/- pi/2 if xy = 1.

2 tan^(-1)x & Telescoping sums: 2 tan^(-1)x = sin^(-1)(2x/(1+x^2)) ONLY for |x| <= 1 (for x > 1, equals pi - sin^(-1)(2x/(1+x^2))). For telescoping series, rewrite tan^(-1)((b - a)/(1 + ab)) = tan^(-1)b - tan^(-1)a when a, b > 0 (or 1 + ab > 0).

derivationsAndGraphs.title: Principal Sawtooth Graphs: arcsin(sin x) & arccos(cos x)
derivationsAndGraphs.expressionOrCurve: arcsin(sin x) = { x in [-pi/2, pi/2]; pi - x in [pi/2, 3pi/2]; x - 2pi in [3pi/2, 5pi/2] }; arccos(cos x) = { x in [0, pi]; 2pi - x in [pi, 2pi] }
derivationsAndGraphs.keyTakeaway: arcsin(sin x) is an odd 2*pi-periodic triangular wave oscillating in [-pi/2, pi/2] with slopes +/- 1; arccos(cos x) is an even 2*pi-periodic triangular wave in [0, pi]. Essential for counting solutions of arcsin(sin x) = kx.

derivationsAndGraphs.title: Step & Sawtooth Decomposition: [x] vs {x}
derivationsAndGraphs.expressionOrCurve: x = [x] + {x}, with 0 <= {x} < 1; graph of {x} has slope +1 on [n, n+1) and jump -1 at every integer n
derivationsAndGraphs.keyTakeaway: Both [x] and {x} are right-continuous and discontinuous at every integer x in Z; equations involving x, [x], and {x} are solved by substituting x = I + f (I in Z, 0 <= f < 1) and bounding f.

derivationsAndGraphs.title: Branch Jump Derivation for tan^(-1)x + tan^(-1)y
derivationsAndGraphs.expressionOrCurve: Let A = tan^(-1)x, B = tan^(-1)y in (-pi/2, pi/2). When x>0, y>0, xy>1 => A + B in (pi/2, pi), while tan^(-1)((x+y)/(1-xy)) lies in (-pi/2, 0)
derivationsAndGraphs.keyTakeaway: Because tan((x+y)/(1-xy)) has the same tangent as A + B but lies 180 deg behind in (-pi/2, 0), adding +pi shifts the principal branch smoothly into (pi/2, pi).

derivationsAndGraphs.title: Symmetry Pairing f(x) + f(1 - x) = 1 & Cauchy Reduction
derivationsAndGraphs.expressionOrCurve: If f(x) = a^x / (a^x + sqrt(a)), then f(1 - x) = a^(1-x) / (a^(1-x) + sqrt(a)) = sqrt(a) / (sqrt(a) + a^x) => f(x) + f(1 - x) = 1
derivationsAndGraphs.keyTakeaway: Any sum Sum_{k=1}^{N-1} f(k/N) pairs symmetric endpoints k and N - k into 1, reducing N - 1 ugly exponential fractions to (N - 1)/2 immediately.

traps: Forgetting the +pi branch correction in tan^(-1)(2) + tan^(-1)(3) yields tan^(-1)(-1) = -pi/4 instead of the true obtuse value 3*pi/4!
Simplifying f(x) = (x^2 - 1)/(x - 1) to x + 1 BEFORE finding the domain misses the hole at x = 1; its domain is R \ {1}, NOT R!
Assuming f(x) = f^(-1)(x) solutions ONLY lie on the line y = x fails for strictly DECREASING functions (e.g. f(x) = 1 - x or -x^3 has off-diagonal intersections (a, b) & (b, a))!
Applying LCM(T1, T2) blindly for period of |sin x| + |cos x| gives pi, missing that f(x + pi/2) = |cos x| + |sin x| = f(x), so fundamental period is pi/2!

Writing 2 tan^(-1)(x) + sin^(-1)(2x/(1+x^2)) = 4 tan^(-1)(x) for all x ignores that for x > 1, sin^(-1)(2x/(1+x^2)) = pi - 2 tan^(-1)(x), making the sum identically constant = pi!

solvedExamples.tag: Concept Builder: Domain & Floor
solvedExamples.question: Find the domain of f(x) = 1 / sqrt([x]^2 - 3[x] - 10) + ln(4 - x^2).
steps: From radical in denominator: [x]^2 - 3[x] - 10 > 0 => ([x] - 5)([x] + 2) > 0.
Since [x] is an integer, [x] <= -3 OR [x] >= 6, which translates to x < -2 OR x >= 6.
From logarithm: 4 - x^2 > 0 => x in (-2, 2).
Take intersection of (x < -2 or x >= 6) with (-2, 2): empty set!
solvedExamples.answer: Empty set (null domain; f is nowhere defined)
solvedExamples.pitfall: Converting [x] > 5 wrongly to x > 5 instead of x >= 6 (since [5.9] = 5 does NOT satisfy [x] > 5)!

solvedExamples.tag: JEE Mains PYQ: ITF Telescoping
solvedExamples.question: Evaluate S = Sum_{r=1}^{10} tan^(-1)(1 / (1 + r + r^2)).
steps: Factor the non-1 part of the denominator: 1 + r + r^2 = 1 + r(r + 1).
Rewrite the numerator 1 as (r + 1) - r so it matches 1 + a*b with a = r, b = r + 1 > 0.
solvedExamples.pitfall: Using tan^(-1)(11) - tan^(-1)(1) without simplifying via tan^(-1)((b-a)/(1+ab)) when options are single inverse-trig terms.

solvedExamples.tag: JEE Mains Fast Shortcut: Symmetry Functional Sum
solvedExamples.question: If f(x) = 4^x / (4^x + 2), evaluate Sum_{k=1}^{19} f(k / 20).
steps: Add f(x) + f(1 - x) = 4^x / (4^x + 2) + 2 / (4^x + 2) = 1 identically for all x in R.
Pair terms (k = 1, 19), (2, 18), ..., (9, 11): 9 symmetric pairs each summing to 1 -> sum = 9.
solvedExamples.pitfall: Forgetting the unpaired middle term k = 10 when N = 20 is even!

solvedExamples.tag: JEE Advanced Multi-Concept: ITF Branch + Bijection
solvedExamples.question: Find the range of f(x) = 2 tan^(-1)(x) + sin^(-1)(2x / (1 + x^2)) for x in R, and find the number of integers in its range.
steps: Recall sin^(-1)(2x / (1 + x^2)) switches branches at |x| = 1: equals 2 tan^(-1)(x) for |x| <= 1, pi - 2 tan^(-1)(x) for x > 1, and -pi - 2 tan^(-1)(x) for x < -1.
For x < -1: f(x) = 2 tan^(-1)(x) - pi - 2 tan^(-1)(x) = -pi identically.
For -1 <= x <= 1: f(x) = 4 tan^(-1)(x), which increases strictly from 4(-pi/4) = -pi to 4(pi/4) = +pi.
For x > 1: f(x) = 2 tan^(-1)(x) + pi - 2 tan^(-1)(x) = +pi identically. Hence Range(f) = [-pi, pi].
solvedExamples.pitfall: Assuming sin^(-1)(2x/(1+x^2)) = 2 tan^(-1)(x) for all x in R gives wrong range (-2*pi, 2*pi) and 13 integers!

sections.heading: Quadratic Equations, Vieta Identities & Newton Power Sums
sections.summary: Beyond root formulas, Vieta relations and depressed transformations solve symmetric root expressions and high-power ratios without ever computing irrational radicals. Newton's recurrence linearly links consecutive power sums S_n = alpha^n + beta^n.
keyPoints: Nature of roots for a x^2 + b x + c = 0 (a != 0): Over R, D = b^2 - 4ac >= 0. Over Q (when a, b, c in Q), roots are rational iff D is a perfect square of a rational, and irrational roots occur in conjugate pairs p +/- sqrt(q).
Real coefficients complex roots: If a, b, c in R and D < 0, roots occur in conjugate pairs p +/- i q. Caution: if coefficients are complex, conjugate root pairing does NOT hold!
Identity vs Equation: An equation a x^2 + b x + c = 0 having MORE than 2 distinct roots must be an identity: a = b = c = 0.
Newton's Identity: For quadratic a x^2 + b x + c = 0 with roots alpha, beta, let S_n = alpha^n + beta^n (or P_n = alpha^n - beta^n). Then a S_n + b S_(n-1) + c S_(n-2) = 0 for all integers n.
Root transformation shortcuts: Replace x -> -x for (-alpha, -beta); x -> 1/x for (1/alpha, 1/beta); x -> x - k for (alpha + k, beta + k); x -> sqrt(x) for (alpha^2, beta^2).
Higher-degree Vieta (cubic a x^3 + b x^2 + c x + d = 0): Sum alpha = -b/a, Sum alpha*beta = c/a, alpha*beta*gamma = -d/a.

sections.heading: Quadratic Graph, Sign & Location of Roots
sections.summary: Evaluating the sign of f(x) = a x^2 + b x + c together with the vertex x_v = -b/(2a) and discriminant D locates roots relative to any threshold k or interval (k1, k2) with 100% precision. Using a * f(k) makes all conditions independent of whether the parabola opens upward or downward.
keyPoints: Parabola vertex & extreme value: Vertex at (-b/(2a), -D/(4a)). f(x) > 0 for all x in R iff a > 0 and D < 0; f(x) < 0 for all x in R iff a < 0 and D < 0.
Both roots strictly greater than k: (1) D >= 0, (2) -b/(2a) > k, (3) a * f(k) > 0. (Reverse vertex inequality to -b/(2a) < k for both roots < k.)
k lies strictly between the two roots (alpha < k < beta): Simply enforce a * f(k) < 0 (guarantees D > 0 automatically, so checking D > 0 is redundant!).
Both roots lie inside open interval (k1, k2): (1) D >= 0, (2) k1 < -b/(2a) < k2, (3) a * f(k1) > 0, (4) a * f(k2) > 0.
Both k1 and k2 lie strictly between the roots (alpha < k1 < k2 < beta): Enforce a * f(k1) < 0 AND a * f(k2) < 0 (guarantees D > 0 automatically).

Exactly one root in (k1, k2): Check f(k1) * f(k2) < 0 (guarantees exactly 1 root in (k1, k2)), PLUS check boundary cases f(k1) = 0 or f(k2) = 0 separately so a root sitting on an endpoint isn't missed or double-counted!

sections.heading: Common Roots, Descartes' Rule & Wavy Curve Inequalities
sections.summary: Two quadratics share one root via cross-multiplication elimination of x^2, or both roots via proportional coefficients. Descartes' rule of signs and wavy-curve intervals cleanly bound real root counts and rational inequalities.
keyPoints: Both roots common between a1 x^2 + b1 x + c1 = 0 and a2 x^2 + b2 x + c2 = 0: iff a1/a2 = b1/b2 = c1/c2 (assuming nonzero denominators).

Exactly one common root (when a1 b2 != a2 b1): Eliminate x^2 by taking a2(eq1) - a1(eq2) to get the common root x_0 = (c1 a2 - c2 a1)/(a1 b2 - a2 b1), yielding condition (c1 a2 - c2 a1)^2 = (b1 c2 - b2 c1)(a1 b2 - a2 b1). Always verify the remaining roots are distinct!
Descartes' Rule of Signs: Number of positive real roots of P(x) = 0 is <= number of sign changes in P(x) (and differs by an even integer); negative real roots <= sign changes in P(-x).

Wavy Curve Method: Factor completely, keep leading coefficients positive, plot critical points on number line, and alternate +/- from right to left EXCEPT at factors with EVEN multiplicity (where sign does NOT flip!).
Denominator exclusion in inequalities: Factors from the denominator can NEVER be included in the solution set even for >= 0 or <= 0 inequalities.
Irrational & Modulus inequalities: sqrt(A) < B <=> A >= 0, B > 0, A < B^2; whereas sqrt(A) > B <=> (A >= 0 and B < 0) OR (B >= 0 and A > B^2).

sections.heading: Complex Algebra: Powers of i, Conjugate, Modulus & Argument
sections.summary: Viewing z = x + iy as an ordered pair (x, y) converts conjugate and modulus identities into vector dot-product and norm rules. Principal argument arg(z) in (-pi, pi] depends on the quadrant of (x, y), NOT merely arctan(y/x).
keyPoints: Powers of i: i^4k = 1, i^(4k+1) = i, i^(4k+2) = -1, i^(4k+3) = -i; sum of ANY 4 consecutive powers of i equals 0.
Conjugate & Modulus laws: z + z_bar = 2 Re(z), z - z_bar = 2i Im(z), |z|^2 = z * z_bar. Parallelogram law: |z1 + z2|^2 + |z1 - z2|^2 = 2(|z1|^2 + |z2|^2).
Purely real vs purely imaginary: z is purely real <=> z = z_bar; z is purely imaginary <=> z + z_bar = 0 (with z != 0).

Principal Argument arg(z) in (-pi, pi]: For z = x + iy (z != 0), let alpha = tan^(-1)|y/x| in [0, pi/2]. Then arg(z) = +alpha (Q1), pi - alpha (Q2), -(pi - alpha) (Q3), -alpha (Q4). Note arg(0) is UNDEFINED!
Argument algebra modulo 2*pi: Arg(z1 z2) = arg(z1) + arg(z2) + 2k*pi (k in {-1, 0, 1} chosen to bring result back into (-pi, pi]); arg(z_bar) = -arg(z) (for z not negative real, where arg = +pi).
Unimodular trick (|z| = 1): Whenever |z| = 1, immediately substitute z_bar = 1 / z to eliminate conjugates algebraically!

sections.heading: Polar/Euler Form, De Moivre's Theorem, Cube Roots (omega) & Triangle Inequality
sections.summary: Euler's representation z = r e^(i theta) turns complex multiplication into scaling plus rotation and yields the Triangle Inequality bounds for geometric optimization. Cube roots of unity 1, omega, omega^2 provide rapid cyclic cancellations in high-degree polynomials.
keyPoints: De Moivre's Theorem: (cos theta + i sin theta)^n = cos(n theta) + i sin(n theta) for all integers n (and one value for rational n); e^(i theta) = cos theta + i sin theta, e^(i pi) + 1 = 0.

Reverse Euler identities: cos theta = (z + 1/z)/2 and sin theta = (z - 1/z)/(2i) for z = e^(i theta); also 1 + e^(i theta) = 2 cos(theta/2) e^(i theta/2) and 1 - e^(i theta) = -2i sin(theta/2) e^(i theta/2).

Cube roots of unity (1, omega, omega^2): omega = (-1 + i sqrt(3))/2 = e^(i 2pi/3). 1 + omega + omega^2 = 0, omega^3 = 1, omega_bar = omega^2 = 1/omega. Sum 1 + omega^k + omega^(2k) = 3 if 3 | k, else 0.

Algebraic factorizations via omega: x^2 + x + 1 = (x - omega)(x - omega^2); x^2 - x + 1 = (x + omega)(x + omega^2); a^3 + b^3 + c^3 - 3abc = (a + b + c)(a + b*omega + c*omega^2)(a + b*omega^2 + c*omega).

Triangle Inequality: ||z1| - |z2|| <= |z1 + z2| <= |z1| + |z2|. Right equality holds iff arg(z1) = arg(z2) (same ray, z1/z2 > 0); left equality holds iff arg(z1) - arg(z2) = +/- pi (opposite rays, z1/z2 < 0).
Optimization on circles: Given |z - z0| <= r, minimum and maximum of |z - w| are max(0, |z0 - w| - r) and |z0 - w| + r respectively (achieved along the line joining z0 and w).

sections.heading: Argand Plane Geometry: Circles, Lines, Ellipses & Ray Loci
sections.summary: Every classical 2D locus has a compact complex coordinate form that avoids expanding x and y unnecessarily. Recognizing perpendicular bisectors, Apollonius circles, and oriented circular arcs turns tedious algebra into two-line geometry.
keyPoints: General Straight Line in C: a_bar z + a z_bar + b = 0 (b in R, a != 0), normal direction along vector a. Perpendicular distance from z0 to this line is |a_bar z0 + a z0_bar + b| / (2 |a|).

Perpendicular bisector & General Circle: |z - z1| = |z - z2| is the perpendicular bisector of segment z1-z2. General circle: z z_bar + a_bar z + a z_bar + b = 0 (b in R) with centre -a and radius sqrt(|a|^2 - b) (real iff |a|^2 >= b).
Apollonius Circle: |z - z1| / |z - z2| = k (k > 0, k != 1) is a circle whose diameter endpoints divide segment z1-z2 internally and externally in ratio k : 1.

Diameter & Circular Arc Loci: Re((z - z1)(z_bar - z2_bar)) = 0 is the circle on z1-z2 as diameter. arg((z - z1)/(z - z2)) = alpha (0 < alpha < pi) is an OPEN circular arc (only on one side of line z1-z2!) subtending angle alpha; if alpha = pi/2, it is a semicircle (not full circle!).
Segment vs Ray vs Exterior Ray: |z - z1| + |z - z2| = |z1 - z2| is the closed line segment z1-z2; ||z - z1| - |z - z2|| = |z1 - z2| is the union of the two exterior rays along line z1-z2.
Conic Loci in C: |z - z1| + |z - z2| = 2a (when 2a > |z1 - z2|) is an Ellipse with foci z1, z2; ||z - z1| - |z - z2|| = 2a (when 0 < 2a < |z1 - z2|) is a Hyperbola with foci z1, z2.

solvedExamples.tag: Concept Builder: Quadratic Location of Roots
solvedExamples.question: Find all real values of k so that both roots of x^2 - 2kx + k^2 + k - 5 = 0 are strictly less than 5.
steps: Leading coefficient a = 1 > 0. Condition (1) D >= 0: (-2k)^2 - 4(1)(k^2 + k - 5) >= 0 => 20 - 4k >= 0 => k <= 5.
Condition (2) Vertex < 5: -b/(2a) = 2k / 2 = k < 5.
Intersect (1) k <= 5, (2) k < 5, and (3) (k < 4 or k > 5): final set is k in (-infinity, 4).
solvedExamples.pitfall: Omitting f(5) > 0 leaves k in [4, 5), which places one root >= 5 even though the vertex stays < 5!

solvedExamples.tag: JEE Mains PYQ: Newton's Power Sums
solvedExamples.question: If alpha and beta are roots of x^2 - 6x - 2 = 0 and a_n = alpha^n - beta^n for n >= 1, find the value of (a_10 - 2 a_8) / (2 a_9).
steps: Since alpha and beta satisfy x^2 - 6x - 2 = 0, multiply by x^8 to get alpha^10 - 6 alpha^9 - 2 alpha^8 = 0 and beta^10 - 6 beta^9 - 2 beta^8 = 0.
Subtract the two equations: (alpha^10 - beta^10) - 2(alpha^8 - beta^8) = 6(alpha^9 - beta^9).
Substitute a_n = alpha^n - beta^n: a_10 - 2 a_8 = 6 a_9.
Divide by 2 a_9 (note a_9 != 0 since alpha != beta): (a_10 - 2 a_8) / (2 a_9) = 6 / 2 = 3.
solvedExamples.pitfall: Solving for irrational roots 3 +/- sqrt(11) and expanding 10th powers wastes 10 minutes and invites arithmetic errors!

solvedExamples.question: If z is a non-zero complex number satisfying |z + 4/z| = 2, find the maximum possible value of |z|.
steps: Apply the reverse triangle inequality: |z + 4/z| >= |z| - |4/z| = |z| - 4/|z|.
Given |z + 4/z| = 2, we get |z| - 4/|z| <= 2.
Check attainability: taking z = (1 + sqrt(5)) i gives z + 4/z = (1 + sqrt(5))i - (sqrt(5) - 1)i = 2i, so |z + 4/z| = 2 holds!
solvedExamples.pitfall: Writing |z + 4/z| <= |z| + 4/|z| gives r^2 - 2r + 4 >= 0, which gives no upper bound!

solvedExamples.question: Let z satisfy |z - 2i| = 2 |z + 2i|. Find the minimum and maximum values of |z| and the complex numbers where they occur.
steps: Square both sides using |w|^2 = w * w_bar or Cartesian x + iy: x^2 + (y - 2)^2 = 4[x^2 + (y + 2)^2].

sections.heading: Matrix Algebra, Trace Properties & Symmetric Decomposition
sections.summary: Matrix multiplication is associative and distributive over addition, but generally NON-commutative (AB != BA) and admits zero divisors (AB = 0 without A = 0 or B = 0). Trace linearity and unique symmetric/skew-symmetric splitting solve structural matrix questions cleanly.
keyPoints: Multiplication & Transpose laws: (AB)^T = B^T A^T (reversal law). Diagonal matrices commute with each other, and A * B = B * A holds only when matrices share special structures (e.g., powers of same matrix or polynomials p(A)).
Trace properties: tr(A) = Sum a_ii; tr(A + B) = tr(A) + tr(B); tr(kA) = k tr(A); tr(AB) = tr(BA) (cyclic invariance: tr(ABC) = tr(BCA) = tr(CAB), though tr(ABC) != tr(BAC) in general!).
Unique decomposition: Every square matrix A = P + Q uniquely where P = (A + A^T)/2 is symmetric (P^T = P) and Q = (A - A^T)/2 is skew-symmetric (Q^T = -Q).

Skew-symmetric essentials: All main diagonal entries of a real skew-symmetric matrix MUST be 0 (hence tr(Q) = 0). Odd-order skew-symmetric determinant is ALWAYS 0; even-order skew-symmetric determinant is a non-negative perfect square.
Power & Similarity tricks: If A = P B P^(-1), then A^n = P B^n P^(-1), det(A) = det(B), and tr(A) = tr(B).
Triangular & Diagonal determinants: Determinant of any upper/lower triangular or diagonal matrix equals the product of its main diagonal entries.

sections.heading: Special Matrices: Orthogonal, Idempotent, Involutory & Nilpotent
sections.summary: Identifying a matrix's defining polynomial equation collapses high powers A^n and complex matrix polynomials into one or two terms. Orthogonal transformations preserve vector lengths and inner products, making rotation matrices trivial to raise to any power.
keyPoints: Orthogonal Matrix (A A^T = A^T A = I): A^(-1) = A^T; |A| = +/- 1 (det +1 = proper rotation, det -1 = reflection). Columns (and rows) form an orthonormal set; if A and B are orthogonal, AB is also orthogonal.
2x2 Rotation Matrix R(theta) = [[cos theta, -sin theta], [sin theta, cos theta]]: Satisfies R(alpha) R(beta) = R(alpha + beta), so R(theta)^n = R(n theta) and R(theta)^(-1) = R(-theta) = R(theta)^T.
Idempotent Matrix (A^2 = A): A^n = A for all n >= 1; |A| in {0, 1} (only invertible idempotent matrix is I). Also I - A is idempotent, and tr(A) equals the rank of A.
Involutory Matrix (A^2 = I): A^(-1) = A; |A| = +/- 1; A^n = I (n even) and A (n odd). Note (I + A)/2 and (I - A)/2 are both idempotent!
Nilpotent Matrix of index k (A^k = 0, A^(k-1) != 0): Always singular (|A| = 0) and tr(A) = 0. Useful binomial trick: if A = I + N with N^k = 0, then A^n = I + n N + C(n,2) N^2 + ... up to N^(k-1)!
Zero-divisor alert: AB = 0 does NOT imply A = 0 or B = 0, EXCEPT when one of them is non-singular (e.g., |A| != 0 and AB = 0 => B = 0). Similarly, AB = AC => B = C ONLY when |A| != 0!

sections.heading: Determinants: Row-Column Operations & Classical Forms
sections.summary: Row and column operations reduce high-degree polynomial determinants to triangular forms without brute-force expansion. Factor theorem on polynomial determinants and standard Vandermonde/Circulant templates give instant factorizations.
keyPoints: Fundamental row/col laws: (1) |A^T| = |A|; (2) Swapping two rows/cols flips sign; (3) Multiplying ONE row by k multiplies |A| by k, so |k A| = k^n |A| for n x n matrix A; (4) R_i -> R_i + m R_j leaves |A| unchanged.
Row-addition linearity trap: You can split a determinant ONLY along ONE row/column at a time; in general |A + B| != |A| + |B|!
Cofactor & False-Cofactor theorem: Sum_j a_ij C_ij = |A| (true expansion), whereas Sum_j a_ij C_kj = 0 for i != k (false expansion using cofactors of another row!).
Vandermonde 3x3 Determinant: det([[1, 1, 1], [a, b, c], [a^2, b^2, c^2]]) = (a - b)(b - c)(c - a). If row 3 is a^3, b^3, c^3, value = (a-b)(b-c)(c-a)(a+b+c).
Circulant 3x3 Determinant: det([[a, b, c], [b, c, a], [c, a, b]]) = -(a^3 + b^3 + c^3 - 3abc) = -(a+b+c)(a^2+b^2+c^2-ab-bc-ca).

Factor Theorem for Determinants: Treat Delta(x) as a polynomial; if setting x = a makes two rows/columns identical or proportional, (x - a) is a factor (and if k rows become identical, (x - a)^(k-1) is a factor!).

sections.heading: Product, Differentiation & Integration of Determinants
sections.summary: Determinants multiply cleanly via |AB| = |A||B|, while differentiating an n x n determinant splits into a sum of n determinants via the product rule. Summation or integration over a single index passes inside ONLY when the other n - 1 rows/columns do not depend on that index.
keyPoints: Product rule for determinants: |AB| = |A| |B| = |BA| for any two n x n square matrices A, B (even when AB != BA).
Determinant Differentiation: For 3x3 Delta(x) with rows R1(x), R2(x), R3(x), d/dx Delta(x) = det(R1', R2, R3) + det(R1, R2', R3) + det(R1, R2, R3') (sum of n determinants for n x n).

Summation & Integration inside Determinant: If ONLY one row (or column) depends on index r (or variable x) while the remaining n - 1 rows are constants w.r.t. r (or x), Sum_r or Integral_a^b distributes straight onto that single row/column!

Multi-row dependence warning: If TWO or more rows depend on r, NEVER distribute Sum_r across each row independently — expand the determinant first or combine rows using operations to isolate r in one row!
Cofactor Matrix & Determinant of Cofactors: If C is the matrix of cofactors of A, then C^T = adj(A), so |C| = |adj(A)| = |A|^(n-1).
Rectangular product determinant: If A is m x n and B is n x m with m > n, then rank(AB) <= n < m, so det(AB) = 0 ALWAYS!

sections.heading: Adjoint & Inverse Golden Chain Identities
sections.summary: Every non-singular n x n matrix satisfies A (adj A) = (adj A) A = |A| I_n, from which an entire hierarchy of adjoint determinants, nested adjoints, and inverse rules follows directly. Mastering this chain turns nested 3x3 adjoint problems into one-line exponent arithmetic.
keyPoints: Fundamental Identity: A (adj A) = (adj A) A = |A| I_n (holds for ALL square matrices A, even when |A| = 0!). If |A| != 0, then A^(-1) = adj(A) / |A|.
Adjoint Determinant Chain (for n x n non-singular A): |adj(A)| = |A|^(n-1); adj(adj A) = |A|^(n-2) A (for n >= 2); |adj(adj A)| = |A|^((n-1)^2); k-nested |adj(adj(...adj A))| = |A|^((n-1)^k).
For 3x3 special values (n = 3): |adj(A)| = |A|^2; adj(adj A) = |A| A; |adj(adj A)| = |A|^4; |adj(adj(adj A))| = |A|^8.

Algebraic Adjoint & Inverse Rules: adj(AB) = (adj B)(adj A) (reversal!); (AB)^(-1) = B^(-1) A^(-1); adj(A^T) = (adj A)^T; (A^T)^(-1) = (A^(-1))^T; adj(k A) = k^(n-1) adj(A); (k A)^(-1) = (1/k) A^(-1).
Commutation with powers: adj(A^m) = (adj A)^m and (A^m)^(-1) = (A^(-1))^m; also adj(A^(-1)) = (adj A)^(-1) = A / |A|.
Singular A adjoint property: If |A| = 0 (n >= 2), then A (adj A) = 0; furthermore, if rank(A) <= n - 2, then adj(A) = 0 identically!

sections.heading: Consistency of Linear Systems (AX = B) & Cramer's Rule
sections.summary: Cramer's determinants Delta, Delta_1, Delta_2, Delta_3 immediately solve unique systems when Delta != 0, but singular cases (Delta = 0) require careful elimination or rank checks to separate infinite solutions from parallel-plane inconsistency.
keyPoints: Cramer's Rule for AX = B (3 equations in 3 variables): x = Delta_1 / Delta, y = Delta_2 / Delta, z = Delta_3 / Delta whenever Delta != 0 (Unique Solution, Consistent).
Singular Non-Homogeneous Check (Delta = 0): If at least one of Delta_1, Delta_2, Delta_3 is NON-ZERO => No Solution (Inconsistent).

The Classic Delta = Delta_1 = Delta_2 = Delta_3 = 0 Trap: Does NOT guarantee infinitely many solutions! Example: parallel planes x + y + z = 1, x + y + z = 2, x + y + z = 3 have ALL four determinants = 0 yet ZERO solutions! Always eliminate variables or check rank([A|B]) vs rank(A).

Rank criterion (Rouche-Capelli): AX = B is consistent iff rank(A) = rank([A | B]). Unique solution iff rank(A) = rank([A|B]) = n; Infinite solutions iff rank(A) = rank([A|B]) = r < n (with n - r free parameters).
Homogeneous System AX = 0: ALWAYS consistent (x = y = z = 0 is the trivial solution). Non-trivial (infinite) solutions exist iff Delta = 0 (for square n x n matrix A).

Geometric meaning of 3 planes in R^3: Unique point (Delta != 0); Line of intersection (rank A = rank[A|B] = 2); Coincident plane (rank = 1); Prism of 3 pairwise intersecting lines or parallel planes (rank A < rank[A|B], inconsistent).

solvedExamples.tag: Concept Builder: Nested Adjoint Scaling
solvedExamples.question: If A is a 3x3 invertible matrix with det(A) = 2, evaluate det(adj(2 adj(A^(-1)))).
steps: Start from inside: det(A^(-1)) = 1 / det(A) = 1/2.
Scale by 2 inside 3x3 determinant: det(2 adj(A^(-1))) = 2^3 * (1/4) = 8 * (1/4) = 2.
Apply outer adjoint for n = 3: det(adj(M)) = det(M)^2 = 2^2 = 4.
solvedExamples.pitfall: Writing det(2 M) = 2 det(M) instead of 2^3 det(M) = 8 det(M)!

solvedExamples.tag: JEE Mains PYQ: Consistency of Linear System
solvedExamples.question: Find the values of alpha and beta for which the system x + y + z = 6, x + 2y + 3z = 10, x + 2y + alpha*z = beta has (i) unique solution, (ii) infinitely many solutions, (iii) no solution.
steps: Compute Delta = det([[1,1,1],[1,2,3],[1,2,alpha]]) = 1(2 alpha - 6) - 1(alpha - 3) + 1(0) = alpha - 3.
Thus for alpha != 3, Delta != 0 => Unique Solution regardless of beta.
When alpha = 3, subtract Eq 2 from Eq 3 directly: (x + 2y + 3z) - (x + 2y + 3z) = beta - 10 => 0 = beta - 10.
If alpha = 3 and beta = 10, Eq 2 and Eq 3 are identical => infinitely many solutions (one free parameter). If alpha = 3 and beta != 10, parallel planes => No Solution.
solvedExamples.answer: Unique: alpha != 3; Infinite: alpha = 3, beta = 10; No solution: alpha = 3, beta != 10
solvedExamples.pitfall: Always subtract/eliminate directly when Delta = 0 instead of blindly computing all three Delta_i!

solvedExamples.tag: JEE Mains Fast Shortcut: Upper-Triangular Nilpotent Power
solvedExamples.question: If A = [[1, 1, 1], [0, 1, 1], [0, 0, 1]], find A^20.
steps: Write A = I + N where N = [[0, 1, 1], [0, 0, 1], [0, 0, 0]] is strictly upper triangular.
Compute N^2 = [[0, 0, 1], [0, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0]] and N^3 = 0 (nilpotent of index 3!).
Since I and N commute, apply Binomial expansion: A^20 = (I + N)^20 = I + 20 N + C(20, 2) N^2.
solvedExamples.pitfall: Forgetting that N^2 adds to the (1, 3) entry alongside 20 * N!

solvedExamples.tag: JEE Advanced Multi-Concept: Matrix Equation + Trace
solvedExamples.question: Let A be a 3x3 matrix such that A^2 - 5A + 7I = 0. If det(A) != 0, express A^(-1) in terms of A and I, and evaluate A^3 in terms of A and I.
steps: Notice from the equation: A^2 = 5A - 7I.
Multiply by A: A^3 = 5 A^2 - 7 A = 5(5A - 7I) - 7A = 18 A - 35 I.
Verification check via trace: if a root satisfies lambda^2 - 5 lambda + 7 = 0, then lambda^3 = 18 lambda - 35 identically.
solvedExamples.pitfall: Dropping the identity matrix I when rewriting 7I or 35I as scalars!

sections.heading: Permutations, Circular Arrangements & Dictionary Rank
sections.summary: Systematic counting separates choices where order matters (permutations) from unordered selections (combinations), handling restrictions cleanly via Gap, Tie-Up, and Total-minus-Unwanted methods. Circular symmetry divides linear arrangements by n (or 2n for reversible garlands).
keyPoints: Alike objects & Gap/Tie-Up methods: Arranging n items with p, q, r identical = n! / (p! q! r!). Never-together items: arrange remaining items first, then place restricted items into the (k + 1) gaps.
Circular Permutations: n distinct objects around a circle = (n - 1)!; if clockwise and anti-clockwise are indistinguishable (garland/necklace), count = (n - 1)! / 2 (for n >= 3).
Selection from alike objects: Number of ways to select >= 0 items from p alike A's, q alike B's, r distinct C's is (p + 1)(q + 1) 2^r (subtract 1 if empty selection is forbidden).

Divisors of N = p1^a1 p2^a2 ... pk^ak: Total divisors = Prod(a_i + 1); Sum of divisors = Prod((p_i^(a_i+1) - 1)/(p_i - 1)); Product of divisors = N^(total_divisors / 2); Number of ways to write N as product of 2 coprime factors = 2^(k - 1).
Legendre's Exponent Formula: Highest power of prime p dividing n! is v_p(n!) = [n/p] + [n/p^2] + [n/p^3] + ... (terminating once p^k > n). Trailing zeros in n! = v_5(n!).

Dictionary Rank Shortcut: Sort letters alphabetically; at each position from left to right, count remaining unused letters strictly smaller than the target letter, multiply by permutations of remaining slots (dividing by factorials of repeated letters including the current slot's multiplicity!), sum and add +1.

sections.heading: Combinations, Grouping, Distributions & Multinomial Method
sections.summary: Distinguishing identical vs distinct objects and identical vs distinct boxes prevents the most common P&C factor errors. Stars-and-bars (Beggar's Method) and generating functions handle all integer-equation constraints effortlessly.
keyPoints: Division into groups of unequal sizes (m + n + p items into sizes m, n, p): (m+n+p)! / (m! n! p!). If k groups have EQUAL size m, divide additionally by k! (only if groups are unlabelled; do NOT divide by k! if distributed to k distinct persons!).
n Distinct objects into r Distinct boxes: Empty allowed => r^n. No box empty (onto) => Sum_{k=0}^r (-1)^k C(r, k) (r - k)^n.
n Identical objects into r Distinct boxes (Beggar's Method): Non-negative integer solutions to x1 + x2 + ... + xr = n is C(n + r - 1, r - 1). Positive solutions (x_i >= 1) is C(n - 1, r - 1).

Upper/lower bounded integer equations: Shift lower bounds first (y_i = x_i - L_i >= 0); handle upper bounds x_i <= U_i via Inclusion-Exclusion or coefficient of x^n in Product (1 + x + ... + x^(U_i)).
Inequality sums x1 + x2 + ... + xr <= n (x_i >= 0): Add a dummy slack variable x_(r+1) >= 0 to convert to equality = C(n + r, r).
Grid paths: Shortest paths on grid from (0, 0) to (m, n) moving only Right/Up = C(m + n, m) = (m + n)! / (m! n!).

sections.heading: Geometrical Counting, Inclusion-Exclusion & Derangements
sections.summary: Geometrical P&C subtracts degenerate collinear or concurrent cases from total selections, while Inclusion-Exclusion resolves multi-restriction complements cleanly. Derangements count permutations leaving zero elements in their original positions.
keyPoints: Lines, Triangles & Diagonals from n points (k collinear): Lines = C(n, 2) - C(k, 2) + 1; Triangles = C(n, 3) - C(k, 3); Diagonals of convex n-gon = n(n - 3)/2; Interior intersections of diagonals (no 3 concurrent) = C(n, 4).
Rectangles vs Squares on m x n chessboard (m horizontal, n vertical grid lines -> (m-1)x(n-1) cells): Rectangles = C(m, 2) * C(n, 2); Squares = Sum_{r=1}^{min(m-1,n-1)} (m - r)(n - r).

Planar Regions: n straight lines in general position (no 2 parallel, no 3 concurrent) divide a plane into 1 + n(n+1)/2 = (n^2 + n + 2)/2 regions; n circles in general position create n^2 - n + 2 regions.
Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion (PIE): |U A_i| = Sum |A_i| - Sum |A_i intersect A_j| + Sum |A_i intersect A_j intersect A_k| - ...; Complement |U A_i|' = |U| - |U A_i|.
Derangement Recurrence & Asymptote: D_n = (n - 1)(D_(n-1) + D_(n-2)) = n D_(n-1) + (-1)^n; ratio D_n / n! rapidly approaches 1/e ~= 0.36788.

sections.heading: Binomial Theorem: General Term, Greatest Term & Remainders
sections.summary: The general term T_(r+1) = C(n, r) x^(n-r) a^r extracts specific powers, rational/irrational term counts, and numerically greatest terms via ratio testing. Rewriting bases as (M +/- 1)^n turns colossal exponential remainders into two-line binomial arithmetic.
keyPoints: General term & middle term: In (x + a)^n, T_(r+1) = C(n, r) x^(n-r) a^r. If n is even, unique middle term is T_(n/2 + 1); if n is odd, two middle terms T_((n+1)/2) and T_((n+3)/2).

Numerically Greatest Term in (x + a)^n: Compute m = (n + 1) / (1 + |x/a|). If m is NOT an integer, unique greatest term is T_([m] + 1); if m IS an integer, BOTH T_m and T_(m+1) share equal maximum magnitude.
Multinomial Theorem: General term in (x1 + x2 + ... + xk)^n is [n! / (r1! r2! ... rk!)] x1^r1 ... xk^rk with r1 + ... + rk = n. Number of distinct terms = C(n + k - 1, k - 1).
Sum of all coefficients: Replace every variable by 1; sum of even-power / odd-power terms of x in P(x) is [P(1) + P(-1)]/2 and [P(1) - P(-1)]/2 respectively.
Divisibility & Remainder trick: Express a^m as k * (b M +/- 1)^p so every term except the last is divisible by M; if final residue is negative, add M to land in [0, M - 1].

Last two digits / Integral part (sqrt(A) + B)^n: For (sqrt(A) + B)^n = I + f (0 < f < 1), let F = (sqrt(A) - B)^n in (0, 1) (when 0 < sqrt(A) - B < 1). Then I + f +/- F is an integer, giving f + F = 1 and proving parity of I!

sections.heading: Binomial Coefficient Identities & Vandermonde Convolutions
sections.summary: Beyond Pascal's identity C(n, r) + C(n, r-1) = C(n+1, r), differentiating/integrating (1 + x)^n and comparing coefficients of x^k in (1 + x)^m (1 + x)^n = (1 + x)^(m+n) resolve complex binomial sums cleanly.
keyPoints: Basic identities: Sum_{r=0}^n C(n, r) = 2^n; Sum of even-indexed = Sum of odd-indexed = 2^(n-1); C(n, r) = (n/r) C(n-1, r-1) (index-absorbing step!).
Linear & Quadratic weighted sums: Sum_{r=0}^n r C(n, r) = n 2^(n-1); Sum r^2 C(n, r) = n(n + 1) 2^(n-2); Sum (-1)^r r C(n, r) = 0 (n >= 2).
Integral / Harmonic Binomial sums: Sum_{r=0}^n C(n, r)/(r + 1) = (2^(n+1) - 1) / (n + 1); Sum (-1)^r C(n, r)/(r + 1) = 1 / (n + 1).
Vandermonde Convolution: Sum_{r=0}^k C(m, r) C(n, k - r) = C(m + n, k) (coefficient of x^k in (1+x)^m (1+x)^n). Special case m = n = k: Sum_{r=0}^n C(n, r)^2 = C(2n, n).
Alternating square sum: Sum_{r=0}^n (-1)^r C(n, r)^2 = 0 (if n is odd), and (-1)^(n/2) C(n, n/2) (if n is even), via coefficient of x^n in (1 - x)^n (1 + x)^n = (1 - x^2)^n.
Hockey-Stick Identity: Sum_{r=k}^n C(r, k) = C(n + 1, k + 1) (derived by repeatedly applying Pascal's rule or coefficient of x^k in Sum (1+x)^r).

sections.heading: Sequences, Telescoping Series & Classical Inequalities
sections.summary: AP, GP, HP, and AGP progressions pair with method-of-differences telescoping to evaluate arbitrary rational and factorial series. Weighted AM >= GM >= HM and Cauchy-Schwarz inequalities find exact minima/maxima when equality holds at symmetric variable values.
keyPoints: AP & GP essentials: T_n = S_n - S_(n-1) (for n >= 2; check T_1 = S_1 separately!). In AP, S_n is quadratic in n with zero constant term: S_n = A n^2 + B n => d = 2A. Sum of infinite GP = a/(1 - r) ONLY for |r| < 1.
Insertion of n means: Between a and b, n AMs have d = (b - a)/(n + 1) (Sum = n*(a+b)/2); n GMs have r = (b/a)^(1/(n+1)) (Product = (sqrt(ab))^n); n HMs have 1/H_k in AP.

AGP & Method of Differences: For AGP Sum (a + (k-1)d) r^(k-1), compute S - r S to reduce to a GP. For V_r polynomials in numerator/denominator, split T_r = V_r - V_(r-1) (e.g., 1/(r(r+1)(r+2)) = (1/2)[1/(r(r+1)) - 1/((r+1)(r+2))], and r * r! = (r+1)! - r!).
Standard Sigma formulas: Sum_{k=1}^n k = n(n+1)/2; Sum k^2 = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6; Sum k^3 = [n(n+1)/2]^2 = (Sum k)^2.

AM >= GM >= HM (STRICTLY for positive reals a_1, ..., a_n > 0): (Sum a_i)/n >= (Prod a_i)^(1/n) >= n / (Sum 1/a_i). Weighted AM-GM: Sum w_i a_i >= Prod a_i^(w_i) for weights Sum w_i = 1, w_i > 0. Equality holds IFF all a_i are equal!
Cauchy-Schwarz & RMS-AM inequalities: (Sum a_i^2)(Sum b_i^2) >= (Sum a_i b_i)^2 (equality iff a_i / b_i is constant); Titu's Lemma: Sum (x_i^2 / y_i) >= (Sum x_i)^2 / (Sum y_i) for y_i > 0.

solvedExamples.tag: JEE Mains PYQ: Dictionary Rank
solvedExamples.question: Find the rank of the word MOTHER in a dictionary formed by all permutations of its letters.
steps: Sort the 6 distinct letters alphabetically: E, H, M, O, R, T.
Words before M (starting with E or H): 2 * 5! = 240. Fix M; remaining: {E, H, O, R, T}.
Words before O (starting with ME or MH): 2 * 4! = 48. Fix O; remaining: {E, H, R, T}.
Words before T (starting with MOE, MOH, MOR): 3 * 3! = 18. Fix T; remaining: {E, H, R}. Words before H (starting with MOTE): 1 * 2! = 2. Fix H; remaining E, R match target.
Total words strictly before MOTHER = 240 + 48 + 18 + 2 = 308 => Rank = 308 + 1 = 309.
solvedExamples.pitfall: Forgetting the final +1 for the word MOTHER itself (answering 308 instead of 309)!

solvedExamples.tag: JEE Mains Fast Shortcut: Telescoping Quartic Sum
solvedExamples.question: Evaluate S_n = Sum_{r=1}^n r / (1 + r^2 + r^4).
steps: Factor Sophie-Germain identity: 1 + r^2 + r^4 = (r^2 + r + 1)(r^2 - r + 1).
Express numerator r = (1/2) [ (r^2 + r + 1) - (r^2 - r + 1) ].
Split term T_r = (1/2) [ 1/(r^2 - r + 1) - 1/(r^2 + r + 1) ]. Note that replacing r -> r + 1 in r^2 - r + 1 gives (r+1)^2 - (r+1) + 1 = r^2 + r + 1!
Telescoping from r = 1 to n cancels all middle terms: S_n = (1/2) [ 1/1 - 1/(n^2 + n + 1) ] = (n^2 + n) / (2(n^2 + n + 1)).
solvedExamples.pitfall: Missing the factorizability of 1 + r^2 + r^4 = (r^2 + r + 1)(r^2 - r + 1)!

solvedExamples.tag: JEE Advanced Multi-Concept: Weighted AM-GM + Binomial Bound
solvedExamples.question: For positive real numbers x, y, z satisfying x y^2 z^3 = 108, find the minimum value of x + 2y + 3z.
steps: To match exponents x^1 y^2 z^3 in the AM-GM product, split 2y into two equal pieces (y + y) and 3z into three equal pieces (z + z + z).
Thus x + 2y + 3z = x + y + y + z + z + z (sum of 6 positive terms!).
Apply AM >= GM to these 6 terms: (x + y + y + z + z + z) / 6 >= (x * y^2 * z^3)^(1/6).
Substitute x y^2 z^3 = 108 = 2^2 * 3^3? Wait: (108)^(1/6). Even if 108 = 4 * 27, 108^(1/6) is achieved when x = y = z = 108^(1/6) (check: x^6 = 108 => valid positive equality!).
solvedExamples.pitfall: Applying AM >= GM directly to (x, 2y, 3z) yields (6 x y z)^(1/3), which fails because the constraint is x y^2 z^3, NOT x y z!

sections.heading: Limits: Indeterminate Forms, Standard Laws & Sandwich Theorem
sections.summary: Existence of limit lim_{x->a} f(x) requires LHL = RHL = finite (independent of f(a)). Recognizing the 7 indeterminate forms (0/0, inf/inf, 0*inf, inf - inf, 1^inf, 0^0, inf^0) and isolating exponential 1^inf limits prevent invalid substitutions.
keyPoints: Standard Trig & Exponential Limits (as x -> 0): sin x / x -> 1; tan x / x -> 1; (1 - cos x) / x^2 -> 1/2; (e^x - 1)/x -> 1; (a^x - 1)/x -> ln a; ln(1 + x)/x -> 1; ((1 + x)^n - 1)/x -> n.
Algebraic infinity limits (x -> +inf or -inf): Divide by highest power of x; watch sign traps like sqrt(x^2) = |x| = -x when x -> -infinity!
1^infinity exponential limit: When f(x) -> 1 and g(x) -> +/- infinity, lim [f(x)]^g(x) = exp( lim (f(x) - 1) * g(x) ). (Do NOT apply if f(x) -> 1+ and g(x) is finite, or if base -> 0 or e!)
0^0 and infinity^0 forms: Take natural logarithm L = exp( lim g(x) * ln f(x) ) and reduce to 0 * infinity -> 0/0 or infinity/infinity.

Sandwich (Squeeze) Theorem: If g(x) <= f(x) <= h(x) near x = a and lim g(x) = lim h(x) = L, then lim f(x) = L. Handles x^2 sin(1/x) -> 0 and floor sums like lim_{n->inf} ([x] + [2x] + ... + [nx]) / n^2 = x / 2.
Limit existence on compositions/products: If lim f(x) = 0 and g(x) is bounded (e.g. sin(1/x)), lim f(x)g(x) = 0 even if lim g(x) DNE!

sections.heading: Maclaurin Series Expansions & L'Hopital Discipline
sections.summary: Taylor/Maclaurin expansions evaluate multi-layer 0/0 limits in seconds where repeated L'Hopital differentiation explodes algebraically. Knowing when L'Hopital fails (oscillatory derivatives or non-indeterminate forms) avoids fatal errors.
keyPoints: Essential Maclaurin Expansions (around x = 0): sin x = x - x^3/6 + x^5/120; cos x = 1 - x^2/2 + x^4/24; tan x = x + x^3/3 + (2/15)x^5.
High-speed cancellation benchmarks: x - sin x ~= x^3/6; tan x - sin x ~= x^3/2; tan x - x ~= x^3/3; e^x - 1 - x ~= x^2/2; sin^(-1)x - x ~= x^3/6.
L'Hopital's Rule prerequisites: Check STRICTLY that form is 0/0 or inf/inf at EVERY step before differentiating numerator and denominator separately (never apply quotient rule!).
When L'Hopital FAILS: If lim f'(x)/g'(x) oscillates without existing (e.g., lim_{x->inf} (x + sin x)/x = 1, while (1 + cos x)/1 oscillates!), L'Hopital is inconclusive — divide by x instead!
Leading-order matching for unknown parameters: To make lim_{x->0} P(x)/x^k finite and non-zero, equate ALL coefficients of x^0, x^1, ..., x^(k-1) in numerator expansion to 0.

sections.heading: Continuity, Discontinuities & Intermediate Value Theorem (IVT)
sections.summary: A function is continuous at x = a iff lim_{x->a-} f(x) = lim_{x->a+} f(x) = f(a) (finite). Piecewise min/max transitions and Intermediate Value Theorem bounds govern existence of roots and jump counts.
keyPoints: Classification of Discontinuities: (1) Removable (LHL = RHL != f(a) or f(a) undefined — hole/isolated point); (2) Jump/First kind (LHL != RHL, both finite); (3) Infinite or Oscillatory/Second kind (limit infinite or oscillates like sin(1/x) at 0).

Algebra of continuous functions: If f, g are continuous at a, then f+/-g, fg, |f|, and f/g (g(a) != 0) are continuous at a. Note: if f is continuous and g is discontinuous at a, f+g is ALWAYS discontinuous, whereas fg MAY still be continuous (e.g. x * sgn(x) = |x| at 0!).

Continuity of Composite f(g(x)): Continuous at a if g is continuous at a AND f is continuous at g(a). Always check BOTH outer discontinuity points (where g(x) hits jump of f) AND inner discontinuity points!

Discontinuity count of [g(x)] and {g(x)}: [g(x)] is discontinuous whenever g(x) crosses an integer (except possible local extrema touching an integer from ONE side only — check whether integer is touched tangentially from above vs below!).
Intermediate Value Theorem (IVT): If f is continuous on [a, b], it attains every value between f(a) and f(b). If f(a) * f(b) < 0, there is AT LEAST ONE root in (a, b).
Fixed-Point Theorem corollary: If f: [a, b] -> [a, b] is continuous, then there exists at least one c in [a, b] such that f(c) = c (apply IVT to g(x) = f(x) - x).

sections.heading: Differentiability: Corners, Smoothing & Composite Rules
sections.summary: Differentiability at x = a requires continuity at a PLUS finite equality of Left-Hand Derivative (LHD) and Right-Hand Derivative (RHD). Sharp modulus corners, cusp tangents, and non-differentiable inner compositions must be tested carefully.
keyPoints: First-principles definition: LHD = lim_{h->0+} [f(a - h) - f(a)] / (-h); RHD = lim_{h->0+} [f(a + h) - f(a)] / h. Differentiable => Continuous (converse is FALSE, e.g. |x| at 0).

Shortcut caveat (using f'(a-) vs f'(a+)): Equal limiting slopes lim_{x->a-} f'(x) = lim_{x->a+} f'(x) = L guarantees f'(a) = L ONLY IF f is ALREADY continuous at a! (For x^2 sin(1/x) at 0, f'(0) = 0 exists even though lim_{x->0} f'(x) DNE!).
Geometric failure modes: (1) Corner (LHD != RHD finite, e.g. |x|); (2) Cusp (LHD = +inf, RHD = -inf, e.g. x^(2/3)); (3) Vertical tangent (LHD = RHD = +inf, e.g. x^(1/3)).

Product smoothing rule: If f is diff at a with f(a) = 0 and g is continuous (not diff) at a, then f(x)g(x) IS differentiable at a (e.g., (x - 1)|x - 1| is diff at 1). If f(a) = 0 AND f'(a) = 0 while g is bounded discontinuous, fg is STILL diff at a (e.g., x^2 sin(1/x) at 0)!
Modulus |f(x)| differentiability: At simple roots of f(x) (f(a) = 0, f'(a) != 0), |f(x)| has a sharp corner (non-diff). At repeated roots (f(a) = f'(a) = 0), |f(x)| IS differentiable at a!

Composite & Piecewise min/max: For f(x) = max{g(x), h(x)}, every intersection g(x) = h(x) where g'(x) != h'(x) creates a non-differentiable corner point. For f(g(x)), inner non-differentiability CAN be killed if outer f'(g(a)) = 0!

sections.heading: Tangents, Normals & Mean Value Theorems (Rolle, LMVT, Cauchy)
sections.summary: Differential geometry of curves relates tangent slopes, subtangents, and orthogonal intersections directly to y'(x). Rolle's Theorem and Lagrange's Mean Value Theorem provide rigorous existence guarantees for roots of f'(x) and function inequalities.
keyPoints: Tangents & Normals at (x1, y1): Tangent slope m = dy/dx|_(x1,y1); Normal slope = -1/m (if m = 0, normal is vertical x = x1). Angle between two curves: tan theta = |(m1 - m2)/(1 + m1 m2)|; orthogonal iff m1 m2 = -1.
Subtangent & Subnormal lengths: Length of Tangent = |y sqrt(1 + (y')^2) / y'|; Normal = |y sqrt(1 + (y')^2)|; Subtangent = |y / y'|; Subnormal = |y y'|.
Parametric & Implicit differentiation: dy/dx = (dy/dt) / (dx/dt); d^2y/dx^2 = [d/dt(dy/dx)] / (dx/dt) (NEVER forget dividing by dx/dt on second derivative!).

Rolle's Theorem: If f is continuous on [a, b], differentiable on (a, b), and f(a) = f(b), there exists at least one c in (a, b) with f'(c) = 0. Corollary: between any two real roots of f(x) = 0, f'(x) = 0 has at least one root!

Lagrange's Mean Value Theorem (LMVT): If f is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b), there exists c in (a, b) such that f'(c) = [f(b) - f(a)] / (b - a). Useful for proving inequalities when f'(x) is bounded: m <= f'(x) <= M => m(b-a) <= f(b)-f(a) <= M(b-a).

Cauchy's Mean Value Theorem: For f, g continuous [a, b], diff (a, b), g'(x) != 0: exists c in (a, b) with [f(b) - f(a)] / [g(b) - g(a)] = f'(c) / g'(c). Auxiliary-function trick: construct h(x) vanishing at multiple points to invoke Rolle on f'(x) + k f(x) = 0 (use h = f e^(kx)).

sections.heading: Monotonicity, Concavity & Global/Local Maxima-Minima
sections.summary: Critical points include BOTH stationary points (f'(x) = 0) AND non-differentiable corner points (f'(x) DNE), alongside interval boundary endpoints for global extrema. Second-derivative sign and concavity tests classify extrema and establish Jensen/convexity inequalities.
keyPoints: Monotonicity criteria: Strictly increasing on interval I if f'(x) >= 0 on I and f'(x) = 0 only at isolated points (e.g., x^3 is strictly increasing on R even though f'(0) = 0!). Strictly decreasing if f'(x) <= 0 similarly.
Critical Points: Points inside Domain(f) where EITHER f'(x) = 0 OR f'(x) does NOT exist (e.g., x = 2 for |x - 2| is a strict local & global minimum!).
First Derivative Test (universal!): At continuous point c, f' changes + to - => Local Maximum; - to + => Local Minimum; no sign change => neither (saddle/inflection).

Second & Higher Derivative Test: If f'(c) = 0 and f''(c) < 0 => Local Max; f''(c) > 0 => Local Min. If f''(c) = 0, find first non-zero f^(n)(c): if n is ODD => neither (inflection); if n is EVEN => Max (f^(n) < 0) or Min (f^(n) > 0).
Global Extrema on closed [a, b]: Compare f(a), f(b), and f(c) at ALL critical points inside (a, b). On open/infinite intervals, check limits as x -> endpoints / +/- infinity.

Concavity, Inflection & Jensen's Inequality: f''(x) > 0 => Concave UP (chord lies ABOVE curve: f(tx + (1-t)y) <= t f(x) + (1-t) f(y)). Inflection point occurs where concavity CHANGES sign (f''(c) = 0 alone is NOT sufficient — e.g. x^4 at 0 has f''(0)=0 yet is NOT an inflection point!).

derivationsAndGraphs.title: Differentiability of x^k sin(1/x) & |f(x)| Corner Graphs
derivationsAndGraphs.expressionOrCurve: f_k(x) = x^k sin(1/x) (x!=0), 0 (x=0): Continuous at 0 iff k > 0; Differentiable at 0 iff k > 1; f'(x) continuous at 0 iff k > 2
derivationsAndGraphs.keyTakeaway: At k = 1, x sin(1/x) is continuous but NOT diff; at k = 2, x^2 sin(1/x) IS diff at 0 (f'(0) = 0) even though lim_{x->0} f'(x) does NOT exist!

derivationsAndGraphs.title: Maclaurin Comparison: x, sin x, tan x Ordering Near 0
derivationsAndGraphs.expressionOrCurve: For x in (0, pi/2): sin x < x < tan x; specifically x - sin x ~ x^3/6 and tan x - x ~ x^3/3 => tan x - sin x ~ x^3/2
derivationsAndGraphs.keyTakeaway: Memorizing the leading x^3 terms eliminates 3 rounds of L'Hopital in 0/0 and 1^infinity trig limits.

derivationsAndGraphs.title: Rolle's & LMVT Geometric Secant-Tangent Slope Map
derivationsAndGraphs.expressionOrCurve: Secant slope [f(b) - f(a)] / (b - a) = f'(c) for some c in (a, b); when f(a) = f(b), tangent at c is horizontal
derivationsAndGraphs.keyTakeaway: If a polynomial has r distinct real roots, its derivative has at least r - 1 distinct real roots; contrapositively, if f'(x) = 0 has k roots, f(x) = 0 has AT MOST k + 1 real roots!

derivationsAndGraphs.title: Concavity & Inflection Sign-Flip Curve (x^3 vs x^4)
derivationsAndGraphs.expressionOrCurve: y = x^3: f''(x) = 6x flips - to + at x = 0 (Inflection!); y = x^4: f''(x) = 12x^2 >= 0 everywhere (Min at 0, NO inflection)
derivationsAndGraphs.keyTakeaway: Never call f''(c) = 0 an inflection point without verifying f'' changes sign across c (or f'''(c) != 0).

formulas.note: Valid ONLY when f(x) -> 1 and g(x) -> +/- infinity
Valid near x -> 0; error is O(x^5)
Also a^x = 1 + x ln a + (x ln a)^2 / 2! + ...
Proved immediately via Squeeze Theorem: nx - 1 < [nx] <= nx
Do NOT forget dividing by x'(t) = dx/dt!
Tangent = |y sqrt(1+y'^2)/y'| ; Normal = |y sqrt(1+y'^2)|
Curves intersect orthogonally iff m1 * m2 = -1
Requires continuity on [a, b] AND differentiability on (a, b)
Requires g'(x) != 0 on (a, b)
Differentiable at f(a) = 0 iff f'(a) = 0
Reverse inequality when f''(x) <= 0 (concave down)

comparison.title: Differentiability Behaviour of Product f(x) * g(x) & Composite f(g(x))
rows: x^2 * sin(1/x) is diff at x = 0 (f'(0)=0)
x * sgn(x) = |x| is NOT diff at x = 0
f(u) = u^2, g(x) = |x| => f(g(x)) = x^2 IS diff!

traps: NEVER apply L'Hopital's rule before verifying 0/0 or infinity/infinity at EVERY stage (applying it to (x+1)/(x+2) or non-indeterminate limits gives wrong answers!).
At local extrema, NEVER discard points where f'(x) does not exist — corners like |x - 2| at x = 2 or x^(2/3) at x = 0 are valid strict minima!
Checking lim_{x->a-} f'(x) = lim_{x->a+} f'(x) WITHOUT first verifying continuity at x = a is invalid (a jump discontinuity with equal left/right slopes is still non-differentiable!).
In x -> -infinity algebraic limits, sqrt(x^2 + x) / x tends to -1, NOT +1, because sqrt(x^2) = |x| = -x for x < 0!
A function with f''(c) = 0 does NOT automatically have an inflection point at c (check y = x^4 at x = 0 where f'' = 12x^2 never changes sign!).

For piecewise [g(x)] continuity, if g(x) merely touches an integer tangentially from ONE side (e.g., [x^2] at x = 0), [g(x)] stays discontinuous at 0 because x^2 >= 0 -> 0 while [-delta] jumps, wait: [x^2] = 0 for x in (-1, 1), so [x^2] IS continuous at x = 0, whereas [-x^2] = -1 for x != 0 and 0 at x = 0 is discontinuous! Always test LHL, RHL, and f(a)!

solvedExamples.tag: Concept Builder: Differentiability Corner Check
solvedExamples.question: Check the continuity and differentiability of f(x) = (x - 1)|x - 1| + |x - 2| at x = 1 and x = 2.
steps: Both terms are continuous everywhere on R, so f(x) is continuous at x = 1 and x = 2.
First term g(x) = (x - 1)|x - 1| equals (x - 1)^2 for x >= 1 and -(x - 1)^2 for x < 1 => g'(1-) = g'(1+) = 0, so g is differentiable everywhere on R.
At x = 1: near x = 1, |x - 2| = 2 - x is linear and differentiable (slope -1). Thus f'(1-) = f'(1+) = 0 - 1 = -1 => f IS differentiable at x = 1.
At x = 2: g(x) is smooth with g'(2) = 2(2 - 1) = 2, while |x - 2| has LHD = -1 and RHD = +1. Thus f'(2-) = 1 != f'(2+) = 3 => f is NOT differentiable at x = 2.
solvedExamples.answer: Continuous everywhere; Differentiable at x = 1, NOT differentiable at x = 2
solvedExamples.pitfall: Assuming every modulus |x - a| creates a corner at x = a misses that multiplying by (x - 1) smooths |x - 1| at x = 1!

solvedExamples.tag: JEE Mains PYQ: Maclaurin Parameter Limit
solvedExamples.question: If lim_{x->0} (a e^x - b cos x + c e^(-x)) / (x sin x) = 2, find the values of a, b, and c.
steps: Denominator x sin x = x (x - x^3/6 + ...) = x^2 + O(x^4).
Expand numerator up to x^2: a(1 + x + x^2/2) - b(1 - x^2/2) + c(1 - x + x^2/2) + O(x^3).
Group powers of x: (a - b + c) + (a - c)x + ((a + b + c)/2)x^2 + O(x^3).
For the limit over x^2 to be finite (= 2): constant = 0 => a - b + c = 0; x-coeff = 0 => a - c = 0 => c = a, b = 2a; x^2-coeff = 2 => (a + 2a + a)/2 = 2 => 2a = 2 => a = 1, b = 2, c = 1.
solvedExamples.pitfall: Using L'Hopital blindly without separating the vanishing conditions at each degree of x!

solvedExamples.tag: JEE Mains Fast Shortcut: 1^Infinity Expansion
solvedExamples.question: Evaluate lim_{x->0} ( (1 + tan x) / (1 + sin x) )^(1 / x^3).
steps: As x -> 0, base (1 + tan x)/(1 + sin x) -> 1 and exponent 1/x^3 -> infinity (1^infinity form).
Apply exponential rule: L = exp( lim_{x->0} [ (1 + tan x)/(1 + sin x) - 1 ] / x^3 ).
Simplify bracket: (tan x - sin x) / (x^3 (1 + sin x)).
Substitute Maclaurin benchmark tan x - sin x ~= x^3 / 2 and 1 + sin x -> 1: exponent = 1/2 => L = e^(1/2) = sqrt(e).
solvedExamples.pitfall: Memorizing tan x - sin x ~= x^3/2 saves 3 tedious applications of L'Hopital's rule!

solvedExamples.tag: JEE Advanced Multi-Concept: Auxiliary Function + Rolle's Theorem
solvedExamples.question: Let f be twice differentiable on R satisfying f(0) = 1, f(1) = 2, and f(2) = 5. Prove that there exists at least one c in (0, 2) such that f''(c) = 2.
steps: Fit the unique quadratic passing through (0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 5): notice P(x) = x^2 + 1 gives P(0) = 1, P(1) = 2, P(2) = 5!
Define auxiliary function g(x) = f(x) - (x^2 + 1), which is twice differentiable on R.
Observe g(0) = 0, g(1) = 0, and g(2) = 0.
Apply Rolle's Theorem to g on [0, 1] and [1, 2] to get c1 in (0, 1) and c2 in (1, 2) such that g'(c1) = 0 and g'(c2) = 0.
Apply Rolle's Theorem to g' on [c1, c2]: there exists c in (c1, c2) subset (0, 2) with g''(c) = 0 => f''(c) - 2 = 0 => f''(c) = 2.
solvedExamples.answer: Proven via g(x) = f(x) - x^2 - 1 and double Rolle's Theorem
solvedExamples.pitfall: Applying LMVT directly only finds points where f'(x) = 1 and f'(x) = 3; subtracting the interpolating quadratic is essential to land on f''(c) = 2!

sections.heading: Indefinite Integration: Standard Forms, Algebraic Twins & By-Parts
sections.summary: Beyond standard primitives and linear substitutions, recognizing structural patterns—Euler's e^x[f(x)+f'(x)], algebraic twins (x^2 +/- 1)/(x^4 + kx^2 + 1), and trig linear quotients—eliminates trial-and-error. Always add constant +C on each connected domain component separately.
keyPoints: Standard quadratic forms: Int dx/(x^2 + a^2) = (1/a)tan^(-1)(x/a); Int dx/(x^2 - a^2) = (1/(2a))ln|(x-a)/(x+a)|; Int dx/sqrt(a^2 - x^2) = sin^(-1)(x/a); Int dx/sqrt(x^2 +/- a^2) = ln|x + sqrt(x^2 +/- a^2)|.

By-Parts (ILATE) & Euler forms: Int u dv = uv - Int v du. Euler specials: Int e^x [f(x) + f'(x)] dx = e^x f(x) + C; generalized Int e^(ax)[a f(x) + f'(x)] dx = e^(ax) f(x) + C; also Int [x f'(x) + f(x)] dx = x f(x) + C.
Algebraic Twins: To integrate (x^2 +/- 1)/(x^4 + k x^2 + 1) dx, divide numerator and denominator by x^2, then substitute t = x -/+ 1/x so dt = (1 +/- 1/x^2) dx matches the numerator!

Trig rational forms: (1) Int dx/(a + b cos x) or (a + b sin x) => substitute t = tan(x/2). (2) Int dx/(a + b cos^2 x + c sin^2 x) => divide by cos^2 x and set t = tan x. (3) (p sin x + q cos x)/(a sin x + b cos x) => write Num = A(Den) + B(d/dx Den).
Irrational algebraic substitutions: Int dx/((px+q)sqrt(ax+b)) => t = sqrt(ax+b); Int dx/((px+q)sqrt(ax^2+bx+c)) => px+q = 1/t; Int dx/((ax^2+b)sqrt(cx^2+d)) => set x = 1/t (or factor x^2).
Reduction & Double-Angle By-Parts: Int sqrt(a^2 - x^2) dx = (x/2)sqrt(a^2 - x^2) + (a^2/2)sin^(-1)(x/a) + C; Int e^(ax) sin(bx) dx = [e^(ax)/(a^2+b^2)] (a sin bx - b cos bx) + C.

sections.heading: Definite Integration: King, Queen, Parity & Periodicity
sections.summary: Most competitive definite integrals do not possess elementary antiderivatives; instead, symmetry reflections (King/Queen) and periodicity collapse messy numerators and denominators into trivial constants. Piecewise integrands with |f|, [x], or {x} must be split at jump/zero points first.
keyPoints: Splitting & Parity: Split at discontinuities/zeros of |f(x)| and [x]. On symmetric [-a, a]: Int_{-a}^a f(x) dx = 0 if f is ODD, and 2 Int_0^a f(x) dx if f is EVEN.

King Property (most important!): I = Int_a^b f(x) dx = Int_a^b f(a + b - x) dx. Always test adding I + I = Int_a^b [f(x) + f(a+b-x)] dx! Works brilliantly on [0, pi/2], [pi/6, pi/3], and symmetric logs.
Queen Property: Int_0^(2a) f(x) dx = Int_0^a [f(x) + f(2a - x)] dx; equals 2 Int_0^a f(x) dx if f(2a - x) = f(x), and 0 if f(2a - x) = -f(x).
Periodic Integral Rules (period T): Int_0^(nT) f(x) dx = n Int_0^T f(x) dx (n in Z); Int_a^(a+T) f(x) dx = Int_0^T f(x) dx (shift invariance); Int_{mT}^{nT} f(x) dx = (n - m) Int_0^T f(x) dx.
Odd-Even trick on [a, b] with e^x: Int_{-a}^a f(x)/(1 + e^x) dx = Int_0^a f(x) dx whenever f(x) is EVEN! (Derived immediately by King x -> -x and noting 1/(1+e^x) + 1/(1+e^(-x)) = 1.)
Classic King benchmark: Int_0^(pi/2) ln(sin x) dx = Int_0^(pi/2) ln(cos x) dx = -(pi/2) ln 2; Int_0^pi x f(sin x) dx = (pi/2) Int_0^pi f(sin x) dx.

sections.heading: Leibniz Rule, Walli's Formula, Inequalities & Riemann Sums
sections.summary: Newton-Leibniz differentiation eliminates integral signs from functional equations, while Walli's reduction computes high trig powers over [0, pi/2] in five seconds. Infinite limits of sums convert directly into definite integrals via r/n -> x.
keyPoints: Newton-Leibniz Derivative Rule: d/dx Int_{g(x)}^{h(x)} f(t) dt = f(h(x)) * h'(x) - f(g(x)) * g'(x) (requires f continuous and g, h differentiable). Note: if x appears INSIDE f(x, t) too, treat x as parameter via Leibniz partial derivative + boundary terms!

Walli's Beta Formula (ONLY on [0, pi/2]): Int_0^(pi/2) sin^m x cos^n x dx = [(m-1)(m-3)... * (n-1)(n-3)...] / [(m+n)(m+n-2)(m+n-4)...] * K, where K = pi/2 if BOTH m, n are even integers (>= 0), else K = 1.
Riemann Sum as Definite Integral: lim_{n->inf} (1/n) Sum_{r = an}^{bn} f(r/n) = Int_a^b f(x) dx. Recipe: identify 1/n -> dx, r/n -> x, lower limit = lim (r_min/n), upper limit = lim (r_max/n).

Product-to-Sum Riemann Trick: For limits of products like lim_{n->inf} [ Prod_{r=1}^n (1 + r^2/n^2) ]^(1/n), take ln L first to turn the product into (1/n) Sum ln(1 + (r/n)^2) -> Int_0^1 ln(1 + x^2) dx!
Definite Integral Bounds: If m <= f(x) <= M on [a, b], then m(b - a) <= Int_a^b f(x) dx <= M(b - a); |Int_a^b f(x) dx| <= Int_a^b |f(x)| dx.
Cauchy-Schwarz Integral Inequality: [Int_a^b f(x) g(x) dx]^2 <= (Int_a^b f(x)^2 dx)(Int_a^b g(x)^2 dx).

sections.heading: Area Under & Between Curves
sections.summary: Geometric area is strictly non-negative, requiring absolute splitting wherever curves cross the axis or intersect each other. Selecting horizontal (dy) vs vertical (dx) strips and applying parabola/inverse-function shortcuts cut calculation time in half.
keyPoints: Area vs Signed Integral: Area bounded by y = f(x), x-axis, x = a, x = b is Int_a^b |f(x)| dx (NEVER forget absolute value when f(x) crosses zero!).
Area between two curves: Vertical strips Int_a^b (y_upper - y_lower) dx; Horizontal strips Int_c^d (x_right - x_left) dy (always choose dy strips for sideways parabolas x = ay^2 + by + c!).

Standard Parabola Area Shortcuts: Area between y^2 = 4ax and x^2 = 4by equals (16 a b) / 3. Area between y^2 = 4ax and line y = mx equals (8 a^2) / (3 m^3). Symmetric parabolic segment of base b and height h has area (2/3) b h!
Ellipse & Circle areas: Area of ellipse x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 = 1 is pi * a * b; area of circle sector of radius R and angle theta is (1/2) R^2 theta.
Inverse Function Area Identity: For strictly monotonic f with f(a) = c, f(b) = d, Int_a^b f(x) dx + Int_c^d f^(-1)(y) dy = b d - a c (difference of outer and inner rectangles!).
Symmetry Exploitation: Check x -> -x (y-axis), y -> -y (x-axis), (x, y) -> (-x, -y) (origin), and x <-> y (y = x) BEFORE integrating to cut limits in half or quarter.

sections.heading: Differential Equations: Order/Degree, Separable & Homogeneous
sections.summary: Order is the highest derivative present, while Degree is well-defined ONLY after clearing radicals and fractions so the equation becomes a polynomial in all derivatives. Variable-separable, homogeneous, and polar differential substitutions cover the core non-linear first-order ODEs.
keyPoints: Order vs Degree: Order = highest derivative order (always defined). Degree = exponent of highest-order derivative AFTER clearing fractional powers/radicals from ALL derivatives. If any derivative sits inside sin(y'), ln(y'), or e^(y'), Degree is UNDEFINED!

Formation of ODE: Eliminating n independent arbitrary constants from a family of curves requires differentiating n times to produce an ODE of order n (count truly independent constants: e.g. y = A e^(x+B) = (A e^B) e^x has only 1 independent constant!).
Variable Separable & Reducible: dy/dx = f(ax + by + c) => substitute t = ax + by + c => dt/dx = a + b f(t), now separable in t and x!
Homogeneous ODEs: dy/dx = f(y/x) (numerator & denominator have identical total degree) => substitute y = v x => dy/dx = v + x (dv/dx), separating x and v cleanly.

Non-Homogeneous Reducible dy/dx = (a1 x + b1 y + c1)/(a2 x + b2 y + c2): If a1/a2 != b1/b2, shift origin to intersection (h, k) via x = X + h, y = Y + k to make homogeneous! If a1/a2 = b1/b2, set t = a1 x + b1 y! Special quick case: if a2 + b1 = 0, cross-multiply to get an EXACT differential!
Polar coordinate shortcuts: Whenever x^2 + y^2 appears alongside x dx + y dy or x dy - y dx, use r^2 = x^2 + y^2 => x dx + y dy = r dr, and tan theta = y/x => (x dy - y dx)/(x^2 + y^2) = d(theta)!

sections.heading: Linear ODEs, Bernoulli, Exact Differentials & Orthogonal Trajectories
sections.summary: First-order linear ODEs dy/dx + P(x)y = Q(x) solve universally via Integrating Factor IF = e^(Int P dx), though switching perspective to dx/dy + P(y)x = Q(y) is often crucial. Exact differential inspection and orthogonal trajectories complete the JEE ODE toolkit.
keyPoints: Linear ODE in y: dy/dx + P(x) y = Q(x) => IF = exp(Int P(x) dx); General Solution: y * (IF) = Int [ Q(x) * (IF) ] dx + C.

Linear ODE in x (often hidden!): If equation is non-linear in y (e.g. contains y^2 or sin y in denominator), invert to dx/dy + P(y) x = Q(y) => IF = exp(Int P(y) dy); Solution: x * (IF) = Int [ Q(y) * (IF) ] dy + C.
Bernoulli Equation: dy/dx + P(x) y = Q(x) y^n (n != 0, 1) => divide by y^n and substitute u = y^(1 - n), so du/dx = (1 - n) y^(-n) dy/dx reduces it directly to linear in u!

Exact Differential Inspection Templates: x dy + y dx = d(xy); (x dy - y dx)/x^2 = d(y/x); (y dx - x dy)/y^2 = d(x/y); (x dy - y dx)/(xy) = d(ln(y/x)); (x dy - y dx)/(x^2 + y^2) = d(tan^(-1)(y/x)); (x dy + y dx)/(xy) = d(ln(xy)).

Orthogonal Trajectories: Given curve family F(x, y, c) = 0, (1) differentiate and eliminate c to get ODE g(x, y, dy/dx) = 0; (2) replace dy/dx with -dx/dy; (3) integrate to find the perpendicular family!
Initial Value & Existence Trap: Apply initial condition y(x0) = y0 ONLY AFTER adding +C; check whether dividing by a term like (y - 1) during separation lost a singular constant solution y = 1!

derivationsAndGraphs.title: King Property Symmetry Cancellation Proof
derivationsAndGraphs.expressionOrCurve: I = Int_a^b f(x) dx = Int_a^b f(a+b-x) dx => 2I = Int_a^b [f(x) + f(a+b-x)] dx

derivationsAndGraphs.title: Inverse Function Area Rectangle Geometry
derivationsAndGraphs.expressionOrCurve: Int_a^b f(x) dx + Int_{f(a)}^{f(b)} f^(-1)(y) dy = b * f(b) - a * f(a) (for strictly increasing f)

derivationsAndGraphs.title: Standard Parabola & Line Enclosed Area Geometry

derivationsAndGraphs.title: Exact Differentials & Orthogonal Slope Field

solvedExamples.tag: Concept Builder: Euler Indefinite Form
solvedExamples.question: Evaluate Int e^x * [ x / (1 + x)^2 ] dx.
steps: Rewrite numerator x = (1 + x) - 1 to separate into two fractions.
Integrand becomes e^x * [ 1/(1 + x) - 1/(1 + x)^2 ].
Notice that if f(x) = 1/(1 + x), then f'(x) = -1/(1 + x)^2!
By Euler's rule Int e^x [f(x) + f'(x)] dx = e^x f(x) + C = e^x / (1 + x) + C.
solvedExamples.pitfall: Applying Integration by Parts twice instead of splitting x = (x + 1) - 1!

solvedExamples.tag: JEE Mains PYQ: King Property Symmetry
solvedExamples.question: Evaluate I = Int_{pi/6}^{pi/3} dx / (1 + sqrt(tan x)).
steps: Apply King property x -> (pi/6 + pi/3) - x = pi/2 - x.
Since tan(pi/2 - x) = cot x = 1 / tan x, we get I = Int_{pi/6}^{pi/3} sqrt(tan x) / (1 + sqrt(tan x)) dx.
Add the original and transformed integrals: 2I = Int_{pi/6}^{pi/3} [ (1 + sqrt(tan x)) / (1 + sqrt(tan x)) ] dx = Int_{pi/6}^{pi/3} 1 dx.
Thus 2I = pi/3 - pi/6 = pi/6 => I = pi/12.
solvedExamples.pitfall: Forgetting to divide 2I by 2 at the end (picking pi/6 instead of pi/12)!

solvedExamples.tag: JEE Mains Fast Shortcut: Newton-Leibniz + Consistency
solvedExamples.question: Let f be a continuous function on R satisfying Int_0^x t f(t) dt = x^2 f(x) - x^4 for all x. Find f(3).
steps: Check x = 0: 0 = 0 (consistent!). Differentiate both sides w.r.t. x via Leibniz + Product Rule:
For x != 0, divide by x: x f'(x) + f(x) = 4x^2, which is exact d/dx(x f(x)) = 4x^2!
Integrate: x f(x) = (4/3) x^3 + C. Letting x -> 0 with continuous f gives 0 = C => f(x) = (4/3) x^2 => f(3) = 12.
solvedExamples.pitfall: Not spotting x f'(x) + f(x) = d/dx(x f(x)) directly!

solvedExamples.tag: JEE Advanced Multi-Concept: Inverse Function Area + Monotonicity
solvedExamples.question: Let f(x) = x^3 + x + 1 for x in R, and let g(x) = f^(-1)(x). Evaluate Int_1^3 f(x) dx + Int_3^31 g(x) dx.
steps: Verify invertibility: f'(x) = 3x^2 + 1 >= 1 > 0 for all x in R, so f is strictly increasing and globally invertible.
Evaluate f at endpoints: f(1) = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3 and f(3) = 27 + 3 + 1 = 31.
Notice the limits of the second integral [3, 31] match [f(1), f(3)] exactly!
Apply the inverse area rectangle identity: Int_a^b f(x) dx + Int_{f(a)}^{f(b)} f^(-1)(y) dy = b f(b) - a f(a).
solvedExamples.pitfall: Attempting to find an explicit formula for f^(-1)(x) of a cubic polynomial, which is completely unnecessary!
