sections.heading: Straight Lines, Point-Line Geometry & Pair of Lines
sections.summary: Parametric distance form x = x1 + r cos theta, y = y1 + r sin theta solves ray-intersection distances rapidly, while family of lines L1 + lambda L2 = 0 handles concurrence without finding intersection coordinates. Angle bisector sign rules separate acute from obtuse bisectors cleanly.
keyPoints: Forms & distances: Point-slope, intercept x/a + y/b = 1, normal x cos w + y sin w = p (p > 0). Distance from (x1, y1) to ax+by+c=0 is |ax1+by1+c|/sqrt(a^2+b^2); parallel lines |c1 - c2|/sqrt(a^2+b^2) (match a, b first!).
Foot of perpendicular (h, k) & Mirror Image (x', y') of (x1, y1) in ax+by+c=0: (x - x1)/a = (y - y1)/b = -K (ax1 + by1 + c)/(a^2 + b^2), where K = 1 for Foot and K = 2 for Image.

Parametric form: (x1 + r cos theta, y1 + r sin theta) represents a point at algebraic distance r along inclination theta; plug directly into line/circle/conic equations to find intercept lengths via Vieta.
Family of concurrent lines: L1 + lambda L2 = 0 passes through L1 intersect L2. Three lines a_i x + b_i y + c_i = 0 are concurrent iff det([a_i, b_i, c_i]) = 0 (or parallel!).

Angle Bisectors of L1: a1x+b1y+c1=0 & L2: a2x+b2y+c2=0 (make c1, c2 >= 0 first!): Bisector containing origin is '+' sign: L1/sqrt(a1^2+b1^2) = +L2/sqrt(a2^2+b2^2). With c1, c2 >= 0: if a1 a2 + b1 b2 > 0, then '+' is OBTUSE bisector and '-' is ACUTE bisector (reversed if a1 a2 + b1 b2 < 0!).

Pair of Straight Lines: Homogeneous ax^2 + 2hxy + by^2 = 0 represents two lines through origin (real iff h^2 >= ab) with tan theta = |2 sqrt(h^2 - ab) / (a + b)|; angle bisectors: (x^2 - y^2)/(a - b) = xy/h. General 2nd degree represents pair of lines iff Delta = abc + 2fgh - af^2 - bg^2 - ch^2 = 0.

sections.heading: Triangle Centres, Euler Line & Locus Techniques
sections.summary: Centroid, Incentre, Circumcentre, and Orthocentre satisfy strict collinearity and reflection properties that eliminate messy perpendicular-bisector calculations. Right-angled and equilateral triangles collapse centres immediately.
keyPoints: Centroid G = ((x1+x2+x3)/3, (y1+y2+y3)/3). Incentre I = ((a x1 + b x2 + c x3)/(a+b+c), ...), where a, b, c are opposite side lengths! Excentre I_1 flips sign of 'a' to '-a'.
Euler Line: In every non-equilateral triangle, Orthocentre (H), Centroid (G), and Circumcentre (O) are collinear with G dividing HO internally in ratio 2 : 1 (HG : GO = 2 : 1 => H + 2O = 3G).

Special triangle shortcuts: (1) Right-angled triangle: Circumcentre O = midpoint of hypotenuse, Orthocentre H = right-angle vertex! (2) Equilateral triangle: G = I = O = H coincide! (3) Lattice-point vertices CANNOT form an equilateral triangle (since Area = (sqrt(3)/4)a^2 is irrational vs rational Shoelace area!).

Reflection of Orthocentre: Mirror image of Orthocentre H in ANY side of triangle ABC lies directly ON the Circumcircle of ABC! Also mirror image of H in midpoint of BC lies on circumcircle diametrically opposite A.
Nine-Point Circle: Passes through midpoints of sides, feet of altitudes, and midpoints of HA, HB, HC; its centre is midpoint of HO and radius = R / 2.

Locus Recipe: Set moving point = (h, k), write geometric condition in terms of (h, k) and parameter t/theta, eliminate parameters cleanly, replace (h, k) -> (x, y), and exclude isolated degenerate holes!

sections.heading: Circles: Chords, Tangents, Orthogonal Circles & Radical Axis
sections.summary: Universal conic notations S, S1, T = 0 unify tangent, chord of contact, pair of tangents, and midpoint-chord formulas for circles and all conics. Circle-pair intersections, common tangent counts, and radical axes simplify coaxial circle families.
keyPoints: General circle x^2 + y^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0: Centre (-g, -f), Radius r = sqrt(g^2 + f^2 - c) (real iff g^2 + f^2 >= c). Diameter form on (x1,y1), (x2,y2): (x-x1)(x-x2) + (y-y1)(y-y2) = 0.

Standard Conic Notations (S = 0): (1) Power S1: point inside if S1 < 0, on if S1 = 0, outside if S1 > 0; (2) Length of tangent from external P = sqrt(S1); (3) Tangent at (x1, y1) on curve & Chord of Contact from external (x1, y1): T = 0; (4) Chord with midpoint (x1, y1): T = S1; (5) Pair of tangents from (x1, y1): S S1 = T^2.
Director Circle of x^2 + y^2 = r^2 (locus of perpendicular tangents): x^2 + y^2 = 2 r^2. Angle between pair of tangents from P at distance d: sin(theta/2) = r / d => tan(theta/2) = r / sqrt(S1).

Common Tangents between two circles (centres d apart, radii r1, r2): d > r1+r2 => 4 (2 DCT, 2 TCT); d = r1+r2 => 3; |r1-r2| < d < r1+r2 => 2; d = |r1-r2| => 1; d < |r1-r2| => 0. Length of DCT = sqrt(d^2 - (r1-r2)^2); TCT = sqrt(d^2 - (r1+r2)^2).
Orthogonal Circles: Two circles cut at 90 deg iff r1^2 + r2^2 = d^2 <=> 2 g1 g2 + 2 f1 f2 = c1 + c2.

Radical Axis & Family of Circles: Radical axis S1 - S2 = 0 (with x^2, y^2 coeffs equal = 1) is ALWAYS perpendicular to the line of centres; three circles have concurrent radical axes (Radical Centre). Family through intersection of circle S and line L: S + lambda L = 0; through two circles: S1 + lambda S2 = 0 (lambda != -1).

sections.heading: Parabola: Parametric Geometry, Focal Chords & Conormal Points
sections.summary: Every parabola y^2 = 4ax reduces cleanly to single parameter t via (a t^2, 2 a t), turning chord slopes, focal chords, and normals into elementary algebra. Tangent intersections at focal chords, reflections, and conormal centroids are top JEE test targets.
keyPoints: Standard forms: y^2 = 4ax (focus (a,0), directrix x = -a), y^2 = -4ax, x^2 = 4ay, x^2 = -4ay. General shifted (y - k)^2 = 4a(x - h) has latus rectum 4a and focal distance of (x1, y1) = |x1 - h + a| (for right-opening).

Chord joining t1 and t2 on y^2 = 4ax: (t1 + t2)y = 2x + 2 a t1 t2. Passes through focus (a, 0) iff t1 * t2 = -1! Focal chord length = a(t1 - t2)^2 = a(t + 1/t)^2 >= 4a (minimum = latus rectum 4a); semi-latus rectum 2a is the HARMONIC MEAN of focal segments l1, l2: 1/l1 + 1/l2 = 1/a.
Tangents to y^2 = 4ax: Slope form y = mx + a/m (contact point (a/m^2, 2a/m)); Parametric form t y = x + a t^2. Tangents at t1, t2 intersect at (a t1 t2, a(t1 + t2)).

Focal Chord Tangent Properties: Tangents at ends of ANY focal chord (t1 t2 = -1) meet perpendicularly (90 deg) right ON the directrix x = -a! Moreover, the circle drawn on ANY focal chord as diameter touches the directrix!

Normals to y^2 = 4ax: Parametric y + t x = 2at + a t^3; Slope form y = mx - 2am - a m^3 (foot (a m^2, -2am)). Normal at t1 meets parabola again at t2 = -t1 - 2/t1; minimum normal chord length = 6 sqrt(3) a (when t1^2 = 2).

Conormal Points (up to 3 normals from (h, k)): Since a m^3 + (2a - h)m + k = 0 is cubic, slopes m1 + m2 + m3 = 0 (sum of ordinates y1 + y2 + y3 = 0, so centroid of conormal triangle lies ON the axis y = 0!). Reflection property: ray parallel to axis reflects through focus; foot of perpendicular from focus onto ANY tangent lies on tangent at vertex x = 0!

sections.heading: Ellipse: Eccentric Angles, Tangents, Normals & Optical Properties
sections.summary: An ellipse x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 = 1 (a > b) compresses the auxiliary circle x^2 + y^2 = a^2 vertically by factor b/a, linking eccentric angle theta directly to chord, tangent, and area properties. Always check whether a > b (horizontal) or b > a (vertical) before writing foci or eccentricity.
keyPoints: Horizontal (a > b) vs Vertical (b > a): For a > b: b^2 = a^2(1 - e^2), foci (+/- a e, 0), directrices x = +/- a/e, latus rectum = 2 b^2 / a, focal distances PF1 = a + e x, PF2 = a - e x => PF1 + PF2 = 2a. For b > a: swap a <-> b and x <-> y!

Auxiliary circle & Eccentric angle: x^2 + y^2 = a^2; parametric point P(a cos theta, b sin theta) (NOTE: theta is eccentric angle, NOT polar angle!). Chord joining theta_1, theta_2: (x/a)cos((t1+t2)/2) + (y/b)sin((t1+t2)/2) = cos((t1-t2)/2).
Tangents to x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 = 1: Point T = 0: x x1/a^2 + y y1/b^2 = 1; Parametric: (x cos theta)/a + (y sin theta)/b = 1; Slope form: y = mx +/- sqrt(a^2 m^2 + b^2).
Director Circle & Tangents Intersection: Director circle is x^2 + y^2 = a^2 + b^2. Tangents at theta_1, theta_2 intersect at ( a cos((t1+t2)/2)/cos((t1-t2)/2), b sin((t1+t2)/2)/cos((t1-t2)/2) ).
Normals to x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 = 1: Point form (a^2 x)/x1 - (b^2 y)/y1 = a^2 - b^2; Parametric a x sec theta - b y cosec theta = a^2 - b^2; Slope form y = mx -/+ [m(a^2 - b^2) / sqrt(a^2 + b^2 m^2)].

Optical & Focal Perpendicular Theorems: (1) Product of perpendiculars from the two foci onto ANY tangent is constant: p1 * p2 = b^2! (2) Feet of focal perpendiculars onto ANY tangent lie on the Auxiliary Circle x^2 + y^2 = a^2! (3) Normal bisects angle F1-P-F2 internally; tangent bisects it externally!

sections.heading: Hyperbola: Asymptotes, Conjugate & Rectangular Hyperbola
sections.summary: Hyperbola x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2 = 1 mirrors the ellipse via b^2 -> -b^2, except its tangent condition requires a^2 m^2 > b^2 and its director circle x^2 + y^2 = a^2 - b^2 is real only when a > b. Asymptotes and rectangular hyperbola xy = c^2 carry high-frequency invariant area properties.
keyPoints: Standard & Conjugate Hyperbola: H: x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2 = 1 has b^2 = a^2(e1^2 - 1), foci (+/- a e1, 0), |PF1 - PF2| = 2a, LR = 2b^2/a. Conjugate C: x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2 = -1 has a^2 = b^2(e2^2 - 1) => 1/e1^2 + 1/e2^2 = 1!

Parametric & Tangents: P(a sec theta, b tan theta). Tangent T = 0; Slope form: y = mx +/- sqrt(a^2 m^2 - b^2) (real tangents exist iff |m| > b/a!). Director circle: x^2 + y^2 = a^2 - b^2 (real iff a > b; single point at a = b; imaginary if a < b!).
Normals: Point form (a^2 x)/x1 + (b^2 y)/y1 = a^2 + b^2; Parametric a x cos theta + b y cot theta = a^2 + b^2; Slope form y = mx -/+ [m(a^2 + b^2) / sqrt(a^2 - b^2 m^2)].
Asymptotes: x/a +/- y/b = 0 (combined A: x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2 = 0). Notice H + C = 2 A (asymptotes sit midway in constant terms!). Angle between asymptotes = 2 tan^(-1)(b/a) = 2 sec^(-1)(e).

Asymptote Tangent Invariants: Any tangent to H intercepted between its two asymptotes is BISECTED at the point of contact, and forms a triangle of CONSTANT AREA = a * b with the asymptotes! Also product of perpendiculars from foci onto any tangent = b^2 (for conjugate sign).

Rectangular Hyperbola (a = b => e = sqrt(2)): Rotated axes form x y = c^2 (where 2 c^2 = a^2), parametric P(c t, c/t). Tangent at t: x/t + y t = 2c; Normal at t: x t^3 - y t = c(t^4 - 1); if normal at t1 meets curve again at t2, then t1^3 * t2 = -1! Orthocentre of ANY triangle inscribed in xy = c^2 lies ON xy = c^2!

sections.heading: Vector Algebra: Linear Combinations, Dot & Cross Products
sections.summary: Vectors translate 3D collinearity, coplanarity, projections, and triangle areas into coordinate-free dot and cross operations. Lagrange's identity links |a x b|^2 and (a . b)^2 cleanly while angle bisectors follow unit-vector addition.
keyPoints: Collinearity & Coplanarity: Three points a, b, c are collinear iff x a + y b + z c = 0 with x + y + z = 0 (not all zero). Four points a, b, c, d are coplanar iff x a + y b + z c + w d = 0 with x + y + z + w = 0.
Dot Product: a . b = |a||b| cos theta. Projection of a on b = (a . b)/|b|; vector component of a along b = [(a . b)/|b|^2] b, and perpendicular to b = a - [(a . b)/|b|^2] b.

Cross Product: a x b = |a||b| sin theta n_hat (anti-commutative b x a = -a x b). Area of triangle with sides a, b = (1/2)|a x b|; Area of parallelogram with adjacent sides a, b = |a x b|, or with diagonals d1, d2 = (1/2)|d1 x d2|.
Lagrange's Identity: |a x b|^2 + (a . b)^2 = |a|^2 |b|^2. Note: vector triple & scalar triple products are excluded from JEE Mains and covered fully in math_adv1.
Internal/External Angle Bisectors between vectors a and b: Along direction (a/|a| + b/|b|) (internal) and (a/|a| - b/|b|) (external).
Unit vector triangle trick: If |a| = |b| = |c| = 1 and a + b + c = 0, then a.b = b.c = c.a = -1/2 (equilateral 120 deg symmetry!); similarly |a +/- b|^2 = |a|^2 + |b|^2 +/- 2(a.b).

sections.heading: 3D Geometry (Lines Focus): Direction Cosines & Skew Lines
sections.summary: In NTA JEE Mains, 3D geometry centres entirely on lines—direction cosines, line-line angles, foot of perpendicular, mirror image, and shortest distance between skew vs parallel lines. Always verify whether two lines are parallel BEFORE applying the skew-line cross product formula.
keyPoints: Direction Cosines (l, m, n) & Ratios (a, b, c): l = cos alpha, m = cos beta, n = cos gamma satisfy l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1 => sin^2 alpha + sin^2 beta + sin^2 gamma = 2. Direction cosines = +/- (a, b, c) / sqrt(a^2 + b^2 + c^2).

Equations of a Line: Vector r = a + lambda b; Symmetric Cartesian (x - x1)/a = (y - y1)/b = (z - z1)/c = lambda (general point (x1 + a lambda, y1 + b lambda, z1 + c lambda)). Always rewrite (2x - 1)/3 into standard (x - 1/2)/(3/2) before reading direction ratios!
Angle between two lines: cos theta = |b1 . b2| / (|b1||b2|); perpendicular iff b1 . b2 = 0; parallel iff b1 = k b2.
Foot of Perpendicular & Image of Point P in Line r = a + lambda b: Let foot M = a + lambda b; enforce (PM) . b = 0 to solve lambda uniquely! Mirror image P' satisfies P' = 2M - P.
Shortest Distance between Skew Lines (r = a1 + lambda b1 and r = a2 + mu b2): d = |(a2 - a1) . (b1 x b2)| / |b1 x b2|. Lines intersect (coplanar) iff d = 0 (and b1 not parallel to b2).
Parallel Lines Distance Trap (b1 = k b2 = b): b1 x b2 = 0, giving 0/0! Use d = |(a2 - a1) x b| / |b| instead! (Note: 3D Planes & Triple Products are in JEE Adv math_adv1.)

sections.heading: Trigonometric Identities, Multiple Angles & Extremum Bounds
sections.summary: Transforming products to sums, telescoping tangent/cotangent series, and bounding a cos x + b sin x cover the trigonometric algebra backbone. Recognizing triangle-angle identities and double-angle cosine chains converts multi-term expressions in one step.
keyPoints: Compound & Multiple Angles: sin(A+/-B), cos(A+/-B), tan(A+/-B); sin(A+B)sin(A-B) = sin^2 A - sin^2 B = cos^2 B - cos^2 A; cos(A+B)cos(A-B) = cos^2 A - sin^2 B.

Triple & Half Angles: sin 3A = 3 sin A - 4 sin^3 A; cos 3A = 4 cos^3 A - 3 cos A; tan 3A = (3 tan A - tan^3 A)/(1 - 3 tan^2 A). Standard 15 deg / 18 deg values: sin 18 = (sqrt(5) - 1)/4, cos 36 = (sqrt(5) + 1)/4, sin 15 = (sqrt(6) - sqrt(2))/4.
Triangle Identities (A + B + C = pi): tan A + tan B + tan C = tan A tan B tan C; cot A cot B + cot B cot C + cot C cot A = 1; sin 2A + sin 2B + sin 2C = 4 sin A sin B sin C.

Cosine Product & Sine/Cosine Arithmetic Progression Sums: cos x * cos 2x * cos 4x ... cos(2^(n-1) x) = sin(2^n x) / (2^n sin x) (when sin x != 0); specially sin theta * sin(60 - theta) * sin(60 + theta) = (1/4) sin 3 theta!
Telescoping Trig Sums: cosec(2 theta) = cot theta - cot(2 theta); tan(A - B) = (tan A - tan B)/(1 + tan A tan B) => tan A tan B = (tan A - tan B)/tan(A - B) - 1.

Harmonic Bound & Quadratic Range: -sqrt(a^2 + b^2) <= a cos x + b sin x <= +sqrt(a^2 + b^2); a sin^2 x + b cosec^2 x >= 2 sqrt(ab) ONLY if b <= a (check equality sin^2 x = sqrt(b/a) <= 1, else minimum at sin^2 x = 1 is a + b!).

sections.heading: Trigonometric Equations & Domain Exclusions
sections.summary: Every trigonometric equation reduces to one of four canonical general-solution templates, followed by careful interval enumeration and domain filtering. Squaring both sides or canceling common factors introduces extraneous or lost roots unless checked explicitly.
keyPoints: Principal & General Solutions: sin x = sin alpha => x = n*pi + (-1)^n alpha; cos x = cos alpha => x = 2n*pi +/- alpha; tan x = tan alpha => x = n*pi + alpha (n in Z).

Squared & Zero Solutions: sin^2 x = sin^2 alpha, cos^2 x = cos^2 alpha, or tan^2 x = tan^2 alpha ALL yield x = n*pi +/- alpha! Special zeros: sin x = 0 => n*pi; cos x = 0 => (2n+1)pi/2; sin x = 1 => 2n*pi + pi/2; cos x = 1 => 2n*pi.
Auxiliary Angle Method (a cos x + b sin x = c): Real solutions exist iff |c| <= sqrt(a^2 + b^2); divide by sqrt(a^2 + b^2) and convert to cos(x - phi) = c / sqrt(a^2 + b^2).
Factorization & Never-Cancel Rule: In sin x cos x = sin x, NEVER divide by sin x (loses x = n*pi)! Bring everything to LHS: sin x (cos x - 1) = 0.
Squaring Trap: If you square sin x + cos x = 1 (or any equation), you MUST plug every candidate root back into the ORIGINAL unsquared equation to reject sign-flipped extraneous roots!

Domain Exclusion & Boundedness: Always reject solutions making tan x, sec x (cos x = 0) or cot x, cosec x (sin x = 0) undefined! For mixed multi-variable equations like sin x + cos y = 2, exploit |sin x| <= 1, |cos y| <= 1 => BOTH must hit +1!

sections.heading: Statistics: Mean, Median, Mean Deviation, Variance & Combined Datasets
sections.summary: Variance and Standard Deviation measure spread relative to the mean and remain strictly invariant under uniform additive shifts, scaling quadratically/linearly under multiplication. Dual-batch combined variance formulas and error-correction adjustments appear reliably in every JEE Mains shift.
keyPoints: Central Tendency & Empirical Relation: Mean x_bar = (Sum f_i x_i) / N; Median M = L + [(N/2 - cf)/f] * h (grouped); Mode = L + [(f1 - f0)/(2f1 - f0 - f2)] * h. Empirical relation: Mode ~= 3 Median - 2 Mean.
Mean Deviation (MD): MD about Mean = (1/N) Sum |x_i - x_bar|; MD about Median = (1/N) Sum |x_i - M| (NOTE: Sum |x_i - a| is MINIMIZED when a = Median!).

Variance & Standard Deviation: sigma^2 = (1/N) Sum (x_i - x_bar)^2 = (1/N) Sum x_i^2 - (x_bar)^2 (shortcut avoids decimal subtraction!). SD sigma = sqrt(sigma^2); Coefficient of Variation CV = (sigma / x_bar) * 100.
Shift & Scale Invariance: If Y = k X + c for every observation, then y_bar = k x_bar + c, SD(Y) = |k| SD(X), and Var(Y) = k^2 Var(X) (additive constant c drops out completely from spread!).

Combined Mean & Variance of two datasets (sizes n1, n2; means x1_bar, x2_bar; variances s1^2, s2^2): Combined mean x_bar = (n1 x1_bar + n2 x2_bar)/(n1 + n2). Combined variance s^2 = [ n1(s1^2 + d1^2) + n2(s2^2 + d2^2) ] / (n1 + n2), where d1 = x1_bar - x_bar, d2 = x2_bar - x_bar.
First n natural numbers benchmark: Mean = (n + 1)/2; Variance of {1, 2, ..., n} = (n^2 - 1) / 12 (so Variance of ANY n consecutive AP terms with common difference d is d^2 (n^2 - 1) / 12!).

sections.heading: Probability: Conditional, Total Probability, Bayes & Binomial Distribution
sections.summary: Distinguishing disjoint (mutually exclusive) events from independent events prevents foundational confusion, while Total Probability and Bayes' Theorem reverse conditional cause-and-effect trees. Discrete random variables and Binomial trials link expectation and variance cleanly.
keyPoints: Addition & Inclusion-Exclusion: P(A U B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A intersect B). P(neither A nor B) = P(A' intersect B') = 1 - P(A U B). P(exactly one of A, B) = P(A) + P(B) - 2 P(A intersect B).
Conditional Probability & Multiplication Rule: P(A | B) = P(A intersect B) / P(B) (P(B) > 0). Chain rule: P(A intersect B intersect C) = P(A) P(B|A) P(C|A intersect B).

Independent vs Mutually Exclusive: A, B independent <=> P(A intersect B) = P(A) P(B) (also A' & B', A & B' are independent; P(A U B) = 1 - P(A')P(B')). Mutually exclusive => P(A intersect B) = 0; two non-zero probability events CANNOT be both independent and mutually exclusive!
Law of Total Probability & Bayes' Theorem: For partition E_1, ..., E_n, P(A) = Sum_k P(E_k) P(A | E_k). Posterior Bayes: P(E_i | A) = [P(E_i) P(A | E_i)] / Sum_k [P(E_k) P(A | E_k)].
Random Variable Mean & Variance: Sum p_i = 1; Mean E(X) = Sum x_i p_i; Variance Var(X) = E(X^2) - (E(X))^2 = Sum x_i^2 p_i - (Sum x_i p_i)^2; Var(aX + b) = a^2 Var(X).
Binomial Distribution B(n, p) (independent Bernoulli trials, q = 1 - p): P(X = r) = C(n, r) p^r q^(n - r); Mean = n p; Variance = n p q (hence Mean > Variance ALWAYS for p in (0, 1)!).

solvedExamples.tag: Concept Builder: Statistics Scaling & Shift
solvedExamples.question: The mean and variance of 5 observations are 10 and 4 respectively. If every observation is multiplied by -2 and increased by 3, find the new mean, new variance, and new standard deviation.
steps: Let new observation Y = -2 X + 3.
New mean y_bar = -2(10) + 3 = -17.
New variance Var(Y) = (-2)^2 * Var(X) = 4 * 4 = 16 (additive shift +3 has zero effect on spread).
New standard deviation SD(Y) = |-2| * sqrt(4) = 2 * 2 = 4 (strictly non-negative!).
solvedExamples.answer: New Mean = -17, New Variance = 16, New SD = 4
solvedExamples.pitfall: Multiplying variance by -2 or 2 instead of (-2)^2 = 4, or returning negative SD!

solvedExamples.tag: JEE Mains PYQ: Shortest Distance Between Skew Lines
solvedExamples.question: Find the shortest distance between the lines (x - 1)/2 = (y - 2)/3 = (z - 3)/4 and (x - 2)/3 = (y - 4)/4 = (z - 5)/5.
steps: Extract points and directions: a1 = (1, 2, 3), b1 = (2, 3, 4); a2 = (2, 4, 5), b2 = (3, 4, 5).
Note b1 and b2 are non-parallel. Compute a2 - a1 = (1, 2, 2).
Norm |b1 x b2| = sqrt((-1)^2 + 2^2 + (-1)^2) = sqrt(6) => Shortest distance d = 1 / sqrt(6).

solvedExamples.tag: JEE Mains Fast Shortcut: Trig Equation Solution Count
solvedExamples.question: Find the number of solutions of cos x + cos 2x + cos 3x = 0 in the interval [0, pi].
steps: Group symmetric outer terms: (cos 3x + cos x) + cos 2x = 0.
Apply sum-to-product: 2 cos 2x cos x + cos 2x = 0 => cos 2x (2 cos x + 1) = 0.
Branch 1: cos 2x = 0 => 2x = pi/2, 3*pi/2 in [0, 2*pi] => x = pi/4, 3*pi/4 (both in [0, pi]).
Branch 2: cos x = -1/2 => x = 2*pi/3 in [0, pi]. Total = 3 distinct solutions.
solvedExamples.pitfall: Expanding cos 3x and cos 2x into a cubic in cos x wastes time and risks algebraic errors!

Two balls are drawn without replacement from the chosen bag and both are found to be white. Find the probability that Bag A was chosen.

sections.heading: Scalar Triple Product [a b c] & Tetrahedron Geometry
sections.summary: The Box Product [a b c] = a . (b x c) computes the signed volume of the parallelepiped spanned by a, b, c and vanishes iff the vectors are coplanar. Cyclic symmetry, linear combination determinants, and Gram-matrix squaring unlock deep IIT Advanced vector inequalities.
keyPoints: Definition & Determinant: [a b c] = a . (b x c) = (a x b) . c = det([a1,a2,a3; b1,b2,b3; c1,c2,c3]). Volume of parallelepiped = |[a b c]|; Volume of tetrahedron with coterminous edges a, b, c = (1/6) |[a b c]|.
Cyclic & Sign Properties: [a b c] = [b c a] = [c a b] (cyclic preserves sign); swapping any two flips sign: [a b c] = -[b a c]. If any two vectors are equal or parallel, [a b c] = 0.
Coplanarity criterion: Three vectors a, b, c are coplanar iff [a b c] = 0. Four points A(a), B(b), C(c), D(d) are coplanar iff [b-a, c-a, d-a] = 0.
Linear Combination Box Identities: [a+b, b+c, c+a] = 2 [a b c]; [a-b, b-c, c-a] = 0 (since (a-b)+(b-c)+(c-a) = 0, linearly dependent!); generally [l1 a+..., ...] = det(coeff matrix) * [a b c].
Gram Determinant (Square of Box Product): [a b c]^2 = det([[a.a, a.b, a.c], [b.a, b.b, b.c], [c.a, c.b, c.c]]), and more generally [a b c][p q r] = det([a_i . p_j]).
Unit Vector Box Bound: For any three unit vectors a, b, c, |[a b c]| <= 1 (maximum 1 iff mutually orthogonal); sum of angles/projections follows directly from the Gram determinant >= 0!

sections.heading: Vector Triple Product (VTP), Four-Vector Laws & Reciprocal Triad
sections.summary: Unlike scalar multiplication, vector cross products are NOT associative: a x (b x c) lies in the plane of b and c, whereas (a x b) x c lies in the plane of a and b. Reciprocal vector triads and cross-product inversion solve vector equations r x a = b instantaneously.
keyPoints: Vector Triple Product (BAC-CAB rule): a x (b x c) = (a . c) b - (a . b) c (vector lies in plane of b and c, perpendicular to a!). Contrast: (a x b) x c = (a . c) b - (b . c) a != a x (b x c) in general!
Jacobi Identity: a x (b x c) + b x (c x a) + c x (a x b) = 0 identically for all vectors a, b, c.

Four-Vector Dot & Cross Products: (a x b) . (c x d) = (a.c)(b.d) - (a.d)(b.c) = det([[a.c, a.d], [b.c, b.d]]). Cross: (a x b) x (c x d) = [a b d] c - [a b c] d = [a c d] b - [b c d] a (lies along intersection line of planes (a,b) and (c,d)!).

Reciprocal System of Vectors (when [a b c] != 0): Define a' = (b x c)/[a b c], b' = (c x a)/[a b c], c' = (a x b)/[a b c]. Key laws: a . a' = b . b' = c . c' = 1; a . b' = 0 (orthogonal to other two); [a' b' c'] = 1 / [a b c]; [a x b, b x c, c x a] = [a b c]^2.
Decomposing any vector r in non-coplanar basis {a, b, c}: r = [r b c]/[a b c] a + [r c a]/[a b c] b + [r a b]/[a b c] c = (r.a')a + (r.b')b + (r.c')c.

Solving Vector Equations: (1) r x a = b (requires a . b = 0 for consistency!) => general solution r = (a x b)/|a|^2 + lambda a; if additionally r . c = alpha (with a . c != 0), cross with c to get unique r = [alpha a + (c x b)] / (a . c)!

sections.heading: 3D Planes: Normal, Intercept, Three-Point & Angle Bisector Planes
sections.summary: A plane ax + by + cz + d = 0 is uniquely fixed by one point and one normal vector n = (a, b, c). Distinguishing normal vectors from line direction vectors prevents the classic cos vs sin angle confusion.
keyPoints: Standard Plane Forms: (1) Point-normal: (r - r0) . n = 0 => a(x - x0) + b(y - y0) + c(z - z0) = 0; (2) Normal form: r . n_hat = p (p >= 0, |n_hat| = 1); (3) Intercept form: x/A + y/B + z/C = 1 (tetrahedron with axes has volume |ABC|/6!).
Plane through 3 non-collinear points a, b, c: [r - a, b - a, c - a] = 0, or det([x-x1, y-y1, z-z1; x2-x1, y2-y1, z2-z1; x3-x1, y3-y1, z3-z1]) = 0.

Point-to-Plane & Parallel Planes Distance: Distance from (x1, y1, z1) to ax+by+cz+d=0 is |ax1+by1+cz1+d|/sqrt(a^2+b^2+c^2). Between parallel planes ax+by+cz+d1=0 and d2=0: |d1 - d2|/sqrt(a^2+b^2+c^2) (match (a, b, c) first!).
Same vs Opposite sides of plane: (x1, y1, z1) and (x2, y2, z2) lie on SAME side iff (ax1+by1+cz1+d) and (ax2+by2+cz2+d) have the SAME sign!
Angle between Two Planes: cos theta = |n1 . n2| / (|n1||n2|); perpendicular iff n1 . n2 = 0; parallel iff n1 = k n2.

Angle Bisector Planes of P1: a1x+b1y+c1z+d1=0 & P2: a2x+b2y+c2z+d2=0 (make d1, d2 >= 0 first!): Origin-containing bisector is '+' sign; with d1, d2 >= 0, '+' is OBTUSE bisector if a1 a2 + b1 b2 + c1 c2 > 0 (and ACUTE if < 0).

sections.heading: Family of Planes, Coplanarity of Lines & Symmetric Intersection
sections.summary: Any plane passing through the line of intersection of two planes P1 = 0 and P2 = 0 takes the single-parameter form P1 + lambda P2 = 0. Converting two intersecting planes into symmetric line form and checking line coplanarity tie 3D lines and planes together.
keyPoints: Family (Pencil) of Planes: P1 + lambda P2 = 0 (plus P2 = 0 itself) represents every plane containing the intersection line of P1 = 0 and P2 = 0.

Line of Intersection in Symmetric Form: Given P1 = 0 (normal n1) and P2 = 0 (normal n2), the line's direction vector is b = n1 x n2; find one common point by setting z = 0 (or x = 0 / y = 0) and solving the 2x2 system!
Coplanarity of Two Lines (r = a1 + lam b1, r = a2 + mu b2): Coplanar iff (a2 - a1) . (b1 x b2) = 0. If non-parallel and coplanar, the unique plane containing BOTH lines is [r - a1, b1, b2] = 0!
Plane containing Line 1 (a1, b1) and Parallel to Line 2 (b2): Simply [r - a1, b1, b2] = 0 (normal is b1 x b2, passing through a1).
Plane containing Point P(r0) and Line (a1, b1): [r - r0, a1 - r0, b1] = 0 (normal is (a1 - r0) x b1).
Plane bisecting segment AB perpendicularly: Normal is (b - a), passes through midpoint (a + b)/2 => (r - (a+b)/2) . (b - a) = 0.

sections.heading: Line-Plane Interactions: Angles, Mirrors, Projections & Oblique Rays
sections.summary: A line with direction b and a plane with normal n make complementary angle theta satisfying SIN(theta) = |b . n| / (|b||n|). Foot, mirror image, line projection, and oblique ray distance all reduce to plugging a parametric ray point into the plane equation.
keyPoints: Line-Plane Angle: sin theta = |b . n| / (|b||n|). Line is PARALLEL to plane iff b . n = 0; Line is PERPENDICULAR to plane iff b = k n.
Line lying COMPLETELY IN plane ax+by+cz+d=0: Requires TWO conditions: (1) b . n = 0 (parallel to plane) AND (2) point (x1, y1, z1) on line satisfies a x1 + b y1 + c z1 + d = 0!

Foot of Perpendicular & Mirror Image of (x1, y1, z1) in plane ax+by+cz+d=0: (x - x1)/a = (y - y1)/b = (z - z1)/c = -K (ax1 + by1 + cz1 + d)/(a^2 + b^2 + c^2), where K = 1 for Foot and K = 2 for Image.

Projection & Image of a Line in a Plane: Find the intersection point Q of line with plane (if not parallel) plus foot/image of ONE other point P on the line; the projected/image line joins Q to the foot/image of P!

Oblique Ray Distance from P(x1,y1,z1) to plane P = 0 measured PARALLEL to direction (l, m, n): Parameterize ray (x1 + l t, y1 + m t, z1 + n t), solve t from P(ray) = 0, then Distance = |t| * sqrt(l^2 + m^2 + n^2)!
Sphere Tangency & Section by Plane (vector form): Sphere |r - c| = R is tangent to plane r . n = d iff |c . n - d| / |n| = R; circle of intersection radius = sqrt(R^2 - p^2).

sections.heading: Advanced 3D Vector Geometry: Common Perpendicular & Tetrahedron Centres
sections.summary: Finding the exact endpoints of the shortest-distance segment between two skew lines and locating tetrahedron centres round out IIT Advanced 3D geometry. Parameterizing both lines and enforcing mutual orthogonality solves the common perpendicular cleanly.
keyPoints: Endpoints of Shortest Distance between skew lines L1(a1 + lam b1) & L2(a2 + mu b2): Take P(lam) on L1 and Q(mu) on L2; solve the two linear equations (PQ) . b1 = 0 AND (PQ) . b2 = 0 for lam and mu!

Equation of Line of Shortest Distance: Passes through P(lam_0) (or Q(mu_0)) with direction vector b1 x b2; also equals the intersection of the two planes [r - a1, b1, b1 x b2] = 0 and [r - a2, b2, b1 x b2] = 0!

Tetrahedron Centroid & Opposite-Edge Sum: For vertices A(a), B(b), C(c), D(d), Centroid G = (a + b + c + d)/4 (joins vertex to opposite face centroid in ratio 3 : 1). Sum of squares of 6 edges = 4 * Sum |G - A|^2.

Regular Tetrahedron benchmarks (edge length L): Height h = L sqrt(2/3); Volume = L^3 / (6 sqrt(2)); Angle between any two faces = cos^(-1)(1/3); Angle between edge and face = cos^(-1)(1/sqrt(3)); Opposite edges are STRICTLY PERPENDICULAR (AB . CD = 0)!
Orthogonal Tetrahedron theorem: If opposite edges AB perp CD and AC perp BD, then AD perp BC automatically, and altitudes are concurrent (orthocentric tetrahedron).
Solving vector systems with cross products: To isolate r from alpha r + r x a = c, dot with a first to find (r . a) = (c . a)/alpha, then cross with a and substitute r x a = c - alpha r!

derivationsAndGraphs.title: Reciprocal Triad Box Proof: [a x b, b x c, c x a] = [a b c]^2
derivationsAndGraphs.expressionOrCurve: Let u = a x b, v = b x c, w = c x a. Compute v x w = (b x c) x (c x a) = [b c a] c - [b c c] a = [a b c] c. Dot with u: (a x b) . ([a b c] c) = [a b c]^2
derivationsAndGraphs.keyTakeaway: Notice v x w collapses in one step using the 4-vector cross identity (p x q) x (r x s) = [p q s]r - [p q r]s; hence reciprocal [a' b' c'] = 1 / [a b c].

derivationsAndGraphs.title: Vector Equation r x a = b & r . c = alpha Inversion
derivationsAndGraphs.expressionOrCurve: Cross r x a = b on the left with c: c x (r x a) = c x b => (c . a) r - (c . r) a = c x b => r = [alpha a + (c x b)] / (a . c)
derivationsAndGraphs.keyTakeaway: Works in 2 lines whenever a . c != 0 and a . b = 0; never decompose into components (x, y, z)!

derivationsAndGraphs.title: Line-Plane Angle (sin theta) vs Plane-Plane Angle (cos theta)
derivationsAndGraphs.expressionOrCurve: Normal n is perpendicular to plane, so angle phi between line b and normal n satisfies cos phi = |b.n|/(|b||n|), giving line-plane angle theta = 90 - phi => sin theta = |b.n|/(|b||n|)
derivationsAndGraphs.keyTakeaway: Always sketch the normal n rising at 90 deg from the plane surface to avoid accidentally using cos theta for line-plane angles.

derivationsAndGraphs.title: Common Perpendicular of Two Skew Lines
derivationsAndGraphs.expressionOrCurve: P = a1 + lam b1, Q = a2 + mu b2 => solve (Q - P).b1 = 0 and (Q - P).b2 = 0 simultaneously
derivationsAndGraphs.keyTakeaway: Gives the exact points P, Q on L1, L2 achieving the minimum distance, the vector equation of the common normal line, and |PQ| directly.

solvedExamples.tag: Concept Builder: Oblique 3D Plane Ray Distance
solvedExamples.question: Find the distance of point P(1, -2, 3) from the plane x - y + z = 5 measured PARALLEL to the line x/2 = y/3 = z/(-6).
steps: Write the ray through P(1, -2, 3) parallel to direction vector (2, 3, -6): Q(t) = (1 + 2t, -2 + 3t, 3 - 6t).
Find where Q(t) pierces the plane x - y + z = 5: (1 + 2t) - (-2 + 3t) + (3 - 6t) = 5.
Compute Euclidean distance PQ = |t| * sqrt(2^2 + 3^2 + (-6)^2) = (1/7) * sqrt(4 + 9 + 36) = (1/7) * 7 = 1 unit.
solvedExamples.pitfall: Computing the perpendicular distance |1+2+3-5|/sqrt(3) = 1/sqrt(3) instead of the oblique distance along (2, 3, -6)!

solvedExamples.question: Find the mirror image of the point P(1, 2, 3) in the plane x + 2y + 4z = 38.

solvedExamples.tag: JEE Mains Fast Shortcut: Vector Equation Inversion
solvedExamples.question: If vector r satisfies r x a = b and r . c = 0, where a . b = 0 and a . c != 0, express r directly in terms of a, b, c.
steps: Take the cross product of r x a = b on the left with c: c x (r x a) = c x b.
Expand LHS via BAC-CAB rule: (c . a) r - (c . r) a = c x b.
Substitute the given orthogonality condition r . c = 0: (a . c) r - 0 = c x b.
Divide by non-zero scalar (a . c): r = (c x b) / (a . c).
solvedExamples.pitfall: Reversing the cross order to (b x c)/(a . c) flips the sign!

solvedExamples.tag: JEE Advanced Multi-Concept: Family of Planes + Parallel Axis
solvedExamples.question: Find the equation of the plane passing through the line of intersection of planes x + y + z = 1 and 2x + 3y - z + 4 = 0, which is parallel to the y-axis; also find its distance from the y-axis.
steps: Write the family of planes P1 + lambda P2 = 0: (x + y + z - 1) + lambda(2x + 3y - z + 4) = 0.
Collect coefficients: (1 + 2 lambda)x + (1 + 3 lambda)y + (1 - lambda)z + (4 lambda - 1) = 0.
Since the plane is parallel to the y-axis (direction j = (0, 1, 0)), its normal is perpendicular to j => y-coefficient = 0: 1 + 3 lambda = 0 => lambda = -1/3.
Distance from any point on y-axis (e.g. (0, 0, 0)) to x + 4z - 7 = 0 is |0 + 0 - 7| / sqrt(1^2 + 4^2) = 7 / sqrt(17).
solvedExamples.answer: Plane: x + 4z = 7 ; Distance from y-axis = 7 / sqrt(17)
solvedExamples.pitfall: Checking x = 0 instead of coefficient of y = 0 when enforcing parallelism to the y-axis!

sections.heading: Argand Rotation Theorem (Coni Method) & Triangle Geometry
sections.summary: Coni's rotation theorem encodes both scaling and oriented angle between two complex segments sharing pivot z0 into a single complex quotient. It yields instant necessary-and-sufficient complex polynomial equations for equilateral, isosceles right-angled, and similar triangles.
keyPoints: Rotation Formula (Coni Method): Rotating vector z1 - z0 counter-clockwise by angle theta and scaling to z2 - z0 gives (z2 - z0)/(z1 - z0) = (|z2 - z0| / |z1 - z0|) * e^(i theta) (use e^(-i theta) for clockwise!).
Collinearity & Perpendicularity: z1, z2, z3 are collinear iff (z3 - z1)/(z2 - z1) is purely REAL; rays z0 z1 and z0 z2 are perpendicular iff (z2 - z0)/(z1 - z0) is purely IMAGINARY.

Equilateral Triangle Condition: Triangle (z1, z2, z3) is equilateral iff z1^2 + z2^2 + z3^2 = z1 z2 + z2 z3 + z3 z1 <=> 1/(z1 - z2) + 1/(z2 - z3) + 1/(z3 - z1) = 0 <=> (z1 - z2)/(z3 - z2) = -omega or -omega^2.
Equilateral Special Case (Origin Centroid): If centroid (z1 + z2 + z3)/3 = 0, then z1^2 + z2^2 + z3^2 = 0 AND |z1| = |z2| = |z3| (circumcentre = centroid).

Similarity of Two Triangles: Triangle (z1, z2, z3) is directly similar (same orientation) to (w1, w2, w3) iff (z3 - z1)/(z2 - z1) = (w3 - w1)/(w2 - w1), equivalently det([[z1, w1, 1], [z2, w2, 1], [z3, w3, 1]]) = 0!

Square & Isosceles Right Triangle: If z1, z2, z3 form an isosceles right triangle right-angled at z2, then (z1 - z2)^2 + (z3 - z2)^2 = 0 (since (z1 - z2)/(z3 - z2) = +/- i). For a square ABCD (anti-clockwise), z3 - z1 = i (z4 - z2) (diagonals equal and perpendicular!).

sections.heading: nth Roots of Unity: Sums, Products & Cyclotomic Factorizations
sections.summary: The n solutions of z^n = 1 sit evenly on the unit circle |z| = 1 as vertices of a regular n-gon, turning trigonometric products and sums into elementary polynomial evaluations. Setting z = 1 or z = -1 in the cyclotomic factorization proves major sine/cosine product formulas in two lines.
keyPoints: Explicit form: Solutions of z^n = 1 are 1, alpha, alpha^2, ..., alpha^(n-1) where alpha = e^(i 2pi/n) = cos(2pi/n) + i sin(2pi/n) (called primitive nth root).
Power Sum & Product Laws: Sum_{k=0}^{n-1} (alpha^k)^m = n if n divides m, and 0 if n does NOT divide m! Product of all n roots = (-1)^(n - 1).
Cyclotomic Factorization: z^n - 1 = (z - 1)(z - alpha)(z - alpha^2)...(z - alpha^(n-1)), so (z^n - 1)/(z - 1) = 1 + z + ... + z^(n-1) = Prod_{k=1}^{n-1} (z - alpha^k).

Setting z = 1 (Distance Product Theorem!): Prod_{k=1}^{n-1} (1 - alpha^k) = n! Geometrically, the product of lengths of all (n - 1) chords/sides from one vertex of a regular n-gon inscribed in a unit circle equals n!

Trigonometric Sine & Cosine Products: Since |1 - e^(i 2pi k/n)| = 2 sin(k pi/n), Prod_{k=1}^{n-1} sin(k pi / n) = n / 2^(n - 1). Similarly Prod_{k=1}^{n-1} cos(k pi / n) = sin(n pi/2) / 2^(n-1) (0 if n even!).
General n-th roots of w = r e^(i theta): z_k = r^(1/n) e^(i (theta + 2k pi)/n) for k = 0, 1, ..., n - 1; they form a regular n-gon on circle |z| = r^(1/n) with sum = 0 (n >= 2).

sections.heading: Advanced Complex Loci: Cross-Ratio, Inversion & Complex Logs
sections.summary: Concyclic four-point conditions, bilinear/Mobius inversions w = 1/z, and principal values of complex powers z^w complete JEE Advanced complex analysis. Cross-ratio reality directly checks whether four Argand points share a common circle or line.
keyPoints: Concyclic 4-Point Cross-Ratio: Four distinct points z1, z2, z3, z4 lie on a circle or straight line iff cross-ratio [(z1 - z3)(z2 - z4)] / [(z1 - z4)(z2 - z3)] is purely REAL (by inscribed-angle theorem!).
Ptolemy's Theorem in C: For any 4 points, |z1 - z3||z2 - z4| <= |z1 - z2||z3 - z4| + |z2 - z3||z1 - z4|, with EQUALITY iff z1, z2, z3, z4 lie in cyclic order on a circle (or line).
Area of Triangle in C: Area(z1, z2, z3) = (1/4) | Im( (z1_bar - z3_bar)(z2 - z3) ) | = (i / 4) * det([[z1, z1_bar, 1], [z2, z2_bar, 1], [z3, z3_bar, 1]]) (unsigned magnitude).
Complex Logarithm & Power: Principal Ln(z) = ln|z| + i arg(z) (-pi < arg(z) <= pi). Principal value of z^w = exp(w Ln z); e.g., i^i = exp(i * (i pi/2)) = e^(-pi/2) (purely real!).

Inversion Mapping w = 1 / z: Maps circles/lines in z-plane to circles/lines in w-plane: circles passing through origin map to lines NOT through origin; lines through origin map to lines through origin!

General Conic / Hyperbola / Ellipse identities: Re(z^2) = c^2 => x^2 - y^2 = c^2 (rectangular hyperbola); |z - z1|^2 + |z - z2|^2 = k => circle around midpoint (z1+z2)/2 provided k >= |z1 - z2|^2 / 2!

sections.heading: Cayley-Hamilton Theorem & High Matrix Powers (2x2 & 3x3)
sections.summary: Every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic polynomial p(lambda) = det(A - lambda I) = 0, converting high matrix powers A^n and matrix inverses A^(-1) into low-degree linear combinations of I, A, and A^2. Polynomial division by the characteristic polynomial solves A^100 instantly.
keyPoints: Characteristic Polynomial: For n x n matrix A, p(lambda) = det(A - lambda I) (or det(lambda I - A) = 0). Cayley-Hamilton Theorem states p(A) = 0 (zero matrix!).
2x2 Cayley-Hamilton (memorize!): A^2 - tr(A) A + det(A) I = 0. Instant inverse (when det(A) != 0): A^(-1) = [tr(A) I - A] / det(A).
3x3 Cayley-Hamilton: A^3 - tr(A) A^2 + (M_11 + M_22 + M_33) A - det(A) I = 0, where M_11 + M_22 + M_33 is the sum of the 3 principal 2x2 minors (Wait: tr(adj A) = M_11 + M_22 + M_33!).
3x3 Inverse from Cayley-Hamilton: A^(-1) = [ A^2 - tr(A) A + tr(adj A) I ] / det(A) (requires det(A) != 0).

Polynomial Division Remainder Shortcut for A^k: To compute f(A) = A^100, divide x^100 by characteristic polynomial p(x) to get x^100 = q(x) p(x) + r(x) (degree < n); since p(A) = 0, f(A) = r(A) identically!
Minimal Polynomial note: If A = k I or A has repeated eigenvalues, A may satisfy an even lower-degree polynomial m(A) = 0 dividing p(A) (e.g., if A is idempotent A^2 - A = 0).

sections.heading: Eigenvalues, Trace/Determinant Links & Matrix Diagonalization
sections.summary: Eigenvalues lambda_1, ..., lambda_n (roots of det(A - lambda I) = 0) govern trace, determinant, invertibility, and polynomial transformations of a matrix simultaneously. Real symmetric matrices guarantee real eigenvalues and orthogonal diagonalizability.
keyPoints: Fundamental Spectral Identities: Sum of eigenvalues = tr(A); Product of eigenvalues = det(A). Matrix A is singular (|A| = 0) iff 0 is an eigenvalue of A.

Algebraic Transformations of Eigenvalues: If lambda is an eigenvalue of A (with eigenvector v), then for any polynomial f(x), f(lambda) is an eigenvalue of f(A); lambda^k for A^k; 1/lambda for A^(-1); |A|/lambda for adj(A); k*lambda for kA.
Transpose & Similarity Invariance: A and A^T share the EXACT same eigenvalues. Similar matrices B = P^(-1) A P have the SAME characteristic polynomial, eigenvalues, trace, determinant, and rank!

Special Matrix Eigenvalue Signatures: Real Symmetric (A^T = A) => ALL eigenvalues are REAL; Skew-Symmetric => purely imaginary or 0; Orthogonal => |lambda| = 1; Idempotent => {0, 1}; Involutory => {+1, -1}; Nilpotent => ALL 0!

Distinct Eigenvalue Diagonalization: If an n x n matrix has n DISTINCT eigenvalues, it is diagonalizable: A = P D P^(-1) where D = diag(lambda_1, ..., lambda_n), making A^k = P D^k P^(-1) and tr(A^k) = Sum lambda_i^k!
Rank-1 Matrix uv^T Shortcut: For column vectors u, v of size n, matrix A = u v^T has rank <= 1, eigenvalues {v^T u, 0, 0, ..., 0}, and satisfies A^2 = (v^T u) A => A^k = (v^T u)^(k-1) A!

sections.heading: Matrix Rank, Row-Echelon Form & Rouche-Capelli System Bounds
sections.summary: Rank measures the true independent dimension of rows or columns of a matrix, resolving rectangular and singular linear systems where Cramer's determinants fail. Sylvester's rank inequality and Rouche-Capelli theorem govern product ranks and solution spaces.
keyPoints: Definition of Rank: rank(A) = number of non-zero rows in Row-Echelon Form = order of largest non-vanishing square minor = dim(row space) = dim(col space). Note rank(A) = rank(A^T) = rank(A^T A).
Elementary Operations Invariance: Elementary row/column operations NEVER change rank(A). For m x n matrix A, 0 <= rank(A) <= min(m, n); rank(A) = 0 iff A = 0.
Product & Sum Rank Bounds: rank(A + B) <= rank(A) + rank(B); rank(AB) <= min(rank(A), rank(B)). Sylvester's Inequality (for m x n A, n x p B): rank(A) + rank(B) - n <= rank(AB).
Zero-Product Rank Constraint: If A (n x n) and B (n x n) satisfy AB = 0, then rank(A) + rank(B) <= n!

Rouche-Capelli Theorem for AX = B (m equations, n unknowns): Consistent iff rank(A) = rank([A | B]). If consistent with common rank r: Unique solution iff r = n; Infinite solutions with (n - r) free parameters iff r < n.
Adjoint Rank Theorem (for n x n matrix A): If rank(A) = n => rank(adj A) = n; if rank(A) = n - 1 => rank(adj A) = 1; if rank(A) <= n - 2 => adj(A) = 0 (rank 0)!

solvedExamples.question: Let A be a 2x2 matrix with tr(A) = 5 and det(A) = 6. Express A^5 - 5 A^4 + 6 A^3 - 2 A + 7 I linearly in A and I.
steps: By Cayley-Hamilton: A^2 - 5A + 6I = 0 identically.
Factor A^3 out of the first three terms: A^5 - 5A^4 + 6A^3 = A^3 (A^2 - 5A + 6I).
Since A^2 - 5A + 6I = 0, the entire cubic-and-higher block vanishes: A^3 (0) = 0!
Therefore A^5 - 5 A^4 + 6 A^3 - 2 A + 7 I = -2 A + 7 I directly.
solvedExamples.pitfall: Computing A^2, A^3, A^4, A^5 individually instead of dividing by the characteristic polynomial A^2 - 5A + 6I!

solvedExamples.question: Let A(z1 = 1 + 2i) and B(z2 = 5 + 5i) be two adjacent vertices of a square ABCD taken in anti-clockwise order. Find the complex numbers z3 (vertex C) and z4 (vertex D).
steps: Compute side vector AB: z2 - z1 = (5 + 5i) - (1 + 2i) = 4 + 3i.
In anti-clockwise square ABCD, vector AD is obtained by rotating vector AB by +90 deg (+pi/2) around pivot A(z1) with equal length.
Apply Coni Rotation Theorem: z4 - z1 = e^(i pi/2) (z2 - z1) = i (4 + 3i) = -3 + 4i.
Since ABCD is a parallelogram/square, vector DC = vector AB => z3 - z4 = z2 - z1 => z3 = (-2 + 6i) + (4 + 3i) = 2 + 9i.
solvedExamples.pitfall: Rotating by -i instead of +i reverses the orientation from anti-clockwise to clockwise!
